utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all in the courtroom. My name is Novak Lukic. Today, I appear for the Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin together with Mr. Stephane Bourgon, who is my co-counsel; our assistant, our legal assistant, Maja Dokmanovic is here with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Now I will briefly summarise our agenda for today. We are now involved in the appeal hearing in the case of the Prosecutor against Mrksic and Sljivancanin. At the outset, I will briefly summarise the appeals which are pending before the Appeals Chamber and the manner in which we will proceed today. The Appeals Chamber deals with Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin's responsibility in relation to the events that took place at Ovcara Farm on 20th and 21st November, 1991. During this time, 194 identified persons from the Vukovar Hospital, the vast majority of whom were shown to be prisoners of war, were mistreated, tortured, and eventually killed. Mile Mrksic, Veselin Sljivancanin, and the Prosecution appeal from the judgement rendered on 27 September 2007, by Trial Chamber II, composed of Judge Parker presiding and Judges Van Den Wyngaert and Thelin. The Trial Chamber found Mr. Mrksic guilty pursuant to Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute for aiding and abetting to murder of 194 persons at the site near the hangar at Ovcara on 20 and 21 November 1991, count 4; aiding and abetting the torture of the prisoners of war at the hangar at Ovcara, count 7; and cruel treatment for having aided and abetted the maintenance of inhumane conditions of detention at the hangar at Ovcara, count 8. The Trial Chamber acquitted Mr. Mrksic on all other counts. The Trial Chamber sentenced Mr. Mrksic to a single term of 20 years' imprisonment. The Trial Chamber found Mr. Sljivancanin guilty pursuant to Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute for aiding and abetting the torture of the prisoners of war held at Ovcara on 20 November 1991, count 7. The Trial Chamber acquitted Mr. Sljivancanin on all other counts. Mr. Sljivancanin was sentenced to a single term of five years' imprisonment. I will now briefly summarise the grounds of appeal. Mile Mrksic brings 11 grounds of appeal. In his first eight grounds of appeal, Mr. Mrksic challenges numerous findings which he claims were entered as a result of the Trial Chamber's failure to apply the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt. Under his ninth ground of appeal, he argues that as a result of the errors alleged in his preceding eight grounds of appeal, the Trial Chamber erred in law in convicting him pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute for having aided and abetted murder, torture, and cruel treatment under Article 3 of the Statute. Under his 10th ground of appeal, Mr. Mrksic disputes certain facts which he claims were not so important for the Trial Chamber in the course of reaching its decision, but which are important to the Defence and the position of the Yugoslav People's Army. Under his 11th ground of appeal, he argues that the Trial Chamber erred in assessing the aggravating and mitigating circumstances when sentencing him to 20 years' imprisonment. Now, if I may, before addressing Mr. Sljivancanin's grounds of appeal, I will briefly touch upon a procedure matter. Given that this concerns confidential filings, can I ask the Court Officer to make arrangements so that we can go into closed session now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I am now turning back to the appeal of Veselin Sljivancanin. He brings six grounds of appeal. Under his first ground of appeal, Sljivancanin argues that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he was present at Ovcara on 20 November 1991. His second ground of appeal alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in law and in fact in its reliance on aiding and abetting by omission. Mr. Sljivancanin's third ground of appeal posits that the Trial Chamber erred by finding that he was in charge of the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital and, thus, that he owed a legal duty to the prisoners of war at Ovcara. In his fourth ground of appeal, Mr. Sljivancanin argues that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he must have witnessed the mistreatment of the prisoners of war at Ovcara. Mr. Sljivancanin's fifth ground of appeal posits that the Trial Chamber erred by finding that his omission substantially contributed to the commission of the crimes and that he must have been aware that through his omission, he facilitated the commission of crimes. Finally, in his sixth ground of appeal, he argues that the Trial Chamber erred by imposing an excessive sentence. The Prosecution brings four grounds of appeal. In its first ground of appeal, it argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law by excluding persons hors de combat from being victims of crimes against humanity and requests the Appeal Chamber to reverse the acquittal of Messrs. Sljivancanin and Mrksic under Article 5 of the Statute and, therefore, first enter a conviction for torture as a crime against humanity under Article 5 of the Statute against Mr. Sljivancanin and, 2, enter convictions for murder, torture, and inhumane acts as crimes against humanity under Article 5 of the Statute against Mr. Mrksic. Under its second ground of appeal, it requests the Appeals Chamber to overturn Mr. Sljivancanin's acquittal for murder and enter a conviction against him under Article 3 of the Statute for having aided and abetted the murder of 194 individuals killed at the grave-site near Ovcara on 20-21 November 1991. As part of its arguments under this ground of appeal, the Prosecution contends that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that Mr. Sljivancanin's legal duty towards the prisoners of war ended upon the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army troops from Ovcara. The Prosecution just submits that Mr. Sljivancanin had a continuing legal duty under international humanitarian law even after Mr. Mrksic ordered the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army troops. The Prosecution's third and fourth grounds of appeal seek to, 1, revise and increase Mr. Sljivancanin's sentence in order to properly reflect the gravity of his criminal conduct; 2, revise and increase Mr. Mrksic's sentence in order to properly reflect the gravity of his criminal conduct; and, 3, revise and increase Messrs. Sljivancanin's and Mrksic's sentences in case the Prosecution's first ground of appeal succeeds; and the Appeals Chamber enters new convictions under Article 5 of the statute. During this appeal hearing, counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in the order they consider most suitable for their presentation, but I would ask them not to just repeat verbatim or to extensively summarise what is in their briefs. I also wish to note that pursuant to the addendum to the scheduling order of 12 December 2008, the Appeals Chamber is inviting the parties to address specific issues during this appeal hearing, issues that do not have to be restated here now. The questions set out in the addendum have been posed, I want to stress, without prejudice to any matter the parties or the Appeals Chamber may wish to raise and in no way constitute an expression of an opinion on the merits of the appeal. I would now like to recall the standard of review applicable to errors of fact and law alleged on appeal. The appeal is not the trial de novo. It is not an opportunity for the parties to re-argue their cases. Rather, in accordance with Article 25 of the Statute, the appellants may limit their arguments -- must limit their arguments to alleged errors of law which invalidate the trial judgement or alleged errors of fact occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Additionally, it should be recalled that the appellants have an obligation to provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments on appeal. I would now turn to the timetable for today's proceedings. This hearing will proceed according to the schedule outlined in the decision on Sljivancanin and Mrksic motions seeking additional time for the presentation of supplementary submissions during the appeal hearing or an alternative remedy and scheduling order for the appeals hearing issued on 25 November 2008. Counsel for Mr. Mrksic will present his submissions this morning for up to one hour and thirty minutes. Following a 15-minutes' pause, the Prosecution will then present its response for up to one hour and thirty minutes. There will then be a one hour and thirty minutes' break, after which counsel for Mr. Mrksic will reply for up to 30 minutes. Counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin will then present his appeal for up to one hour and thirty minutes. Following a 15-minute pause, the Prosecution will present its response for one hour and thirty minutes to finish today's proceedings. The hearing will then continue on Friday, starting with Mr. Sljivancanin's reply and continuing on to the Prosecution's appeal. I would note for counsels' benefit that the time-limits I have mentioned are the maximums allowed. There is no requirement that they use all the time that they are allowed. It would be most helpful to the Appeals Chamber if the parties could present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. I wish to remind the parties that the Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions, or they may prefer to ask questions following each party's submission. Having said this about the manner in which we will proceed today, I would now like to invite counsel for Mr. Mrksic to present submissions in support of his appeal. Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Mile Mrksic fully abides by all its 11 grounds of appeal. However, within its oral presentation within the time-limits provided, it will focus only on the most important parts of the appeal. First of all, one should state that the judgement that is being looked at here through the appeals of all parties in the proceedings is the result of the decision made by the Trial Chamber to deviate from the principle of establishing facts beyond reasonable doubt and decide to make conclusions that are based on a sentence referred to in paragraph 321 of the judgement, and that is: Such an order only could have come from Mile Mrksic. In addition to all the statements to the effect of what the authority of the security organs was, and Captain Karanfilov belonged to them and he conveyed the order on withdrawal, and they had a separate line of command, and the Trial Chamber deals with that in paragraph 285 in the judgement, the mentioned conclusion on the responsibility of Mile Mrksic for issuing an order to have the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade withdraw from Ovcara Farm seems controversial. It seems to be based on the principle: Who was it if it wasn't him? There is no evidence that would lead any reasonable Trial Chamber to reach such a decision. The Trial Chamber, as they tried to establish a logical connection between such a conclusion and the adduced evidence, they had to accept the statements of witnesses whom they, themselves, find not to be telling the truth, and that is evident. These witnesses were concealing their personal responsibility or the responsibility of their friends and comrades-at-arms. I am referring here to the statements of Witnesses Vojnovic, Vukosavljevic, Panic, Vukasinovic, Karanfilov, Vujic, Susic, and Trifunovic. The Trial Chamber, as they made such a decision, they had to reject the logic of material evidence like Exhibits 371, 375, 419 [Realtime transcript read in error, "429"], 268 and 269 [Realtime transcript read in error] respectively, as well as many others. They concluded that witness statements were more reliable than documents that were undeniably created at the time and at the place that is of relevance here. Witness statements that the Trial Chamber refers to in this context are precisely those that belong to the category that we discussed a few moments ago. In order for the conclusions on the guilt of Mile Mrksic to subsist in this kind of a system of legal conclusions, the Trial Chamber had to give up on the establishment of chronology and cause and consequence, in terms of particular events. In the judgement, in paragraph 321, the Trial Chamber, after the proceedings were concluded, does not establish precisely who it was that issued the order if it wasn't Mr. Mrksic. They don't know when the order was issued, before or after the daily briefing, and at what time this happened. They don't know for what reason the security was withdrawn. This unrelenting game of questions cannot lead to the conclusion that it's only Mrksic himself who knows the answer. The only thing that the Trial Chamber establishes precisely is that the withdrawal took place before 9.00 p.m., although in the operations log of the 80th Motorised Brigade, Exhibit 371, as for the 20th of November, 1991, it says that the security detail withdrew at 2235 hours precisely. I just want to say that it doesn't say that it says "2200 hours," "2230 hours," but, rather, it says "2235 hours," so if someone were inventing things, would it be that way? Would it be in such terms of time? The Trial Chamber establishes that Mile Mrksic was commander of Operations Group South and that all other units were subordinated to him. However, that cannot be grounds -- or, rather, the only ground for establishing that he issued the order on the withdrawal of the units of the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade from the hangar at the Ovcara Farm because according to the principle which was applied in the trial judgement, this order could have been issued by any officer from the security line, the security chain all the way up to the top, or any officer of the Command of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Responsibility for the security of the area in which there is no civilian authority, as was the case in Vukovar and the surrounding area in November 1991, according to the decision of the Supreme Command and the Command of the 1st military district, lay in the hands of the town commands, which constituted the military authority in these regions and that were established to protect the property and persons in these territories as well as prisoners of war if they happened to be in these areas. The responsibility of the commander of the town stems from the authority vested in him in the Rules of Service in Article 72 and 78, speaking of the tasks of the commands of garrisons and commands of barracks. The Supreme Command was aware of the fact that it is only in this way, by creating town commands at lower levels, can the safety and security of property and persons be protected until civilian authority is re-established. That is why Mile Mrksic, through his own order, appointed the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade to be the commander of the area of Jakobovac, Ovcara, and Grabovo with all the duties aforementioned resubordinating to him for these needs more than 1.000 soldiers and pieces of armoured equipment. In addition to this, Exhibit 375 of the war diary of the 80th Motorised Brigade shows that Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic was given the task on the 19th of November, 1991, to prepare his unit for guarding prisoners of war from the area of the hospital at Ovcara on the day of the 20th of November, 1991. Bearing this in mind, the conclusion of the Trial Chamber, as referred to in paragraph 316 of the judgement as some kind of surprise of Commander Vojnovic and his unit, cannot be established beyond reasonable doubt or would any reasonable trier of fact and that this kind of order that was entered into the war diary could have remained something unknown to the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Finally, the Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic testified to the fact that his unit had this task and was preparing for it. As for assessing what is written in the war diary, the Trial Chamber in this case and in some other cases establishes that the entries that were made in -- or, rather, at the time when the events concerned happened are not updated, and therefore, the Trial Chamber does not accept them as accurate. However, the party in charge of the accuracy of the documents, and that is the Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic, he fully confirmed the correctness and the fact that the documents of the 80th Motorised Brigade were kept up to date. Finally, the documents that we're discussing here, the war diary and the operations diary, were kept by two different persons. Both of them were intellectuals and pedantic in terms of their work. One was the manager of a company. The other one was a JNA major. The correctness of these entries and the fact that the security organs were in charge of triage and transport and that the 80th Motorised Brigade was given the task to guard the prisoners at Ovcara is attested to by the fact that at the moment when the buses started arriving in Ovcara, first and foremost, there was Commander Vojnovic there, and the commander of Ovcara, and the unit of the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and the Chief of Staff of Operations Group South, and Major Vukasinovic, who led the convoy, and Captain -- and the captain who was in charge of the group of prisoners of war from Mitnica on the 18th of November, 1991, and a large group of security officers from the security administration, and members of the counter-intelligence group from Sid. The security organs were taking JNA soldiers out of the bus, those who were of Croat ethnicity, and they testified here. They were taken off the bus, and the commander of Operations Group South was not questioned -- was not asked about this at all. There is a security colonel with a car there and who was watching all of this, and also, the men who were sent there by the chief of the security administration, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, were there too. As for these facts, it is hard for any reasonable trier of fact to conclude that Mrksic suddenly ordered a change of destination and that he sent the prisoners of war to Ovcara rather than to Sremska Mitrovica. That is referred to in paragraph 610 to 612 of the judgement. Mrksic did not make such a decision because he was not in charge of dealing with prisoners of war. The Trial Chamber, in order to bring -- or to link Mile Mrksic together with the fate of the prisoners of war, took the statement of Witness Panic on his presence at the so-called government meeting. This sequence of events and the statement by Witness Panic does not fit into the time and events that took place on that day in Vukovar, so the Trial Chamber also changes the timing of the events, although the material events in Exhibits 268 and 269, representing the crucial material, it was proved that at the time when the Trial Chamber found that the meeting took place, Slavko Dokmanovic, who was present at the meeting, happened to be with the delegation from Kladovo in Backa Palanka and later was on his way to Vukovar. In the film which these exhibits are, 268 and 269, you can see that this delegation arrived in the courtyard of Velepromet sometime before 1400 hours. Supporting these material facts or this material evidence, the Prosecution -- well, you can also include the Prosecution exhibits which were admitted under Rule 92 bis, and these are the statements of ministers in the so-called government which confirmed the authenticity of the film, but the problem is not just this but the fact that the conclusions of the Trial Chamber based on the testimony of Witness Panic, about whom the Chamber itself found that for the most part in his testimony he did not speak the truth, and this is something that the Defence dealt with in its paragraphs 201 to 224 of its appeal. I would just like to emphasise one fact here, and that has to do with this issue of what Mrksic said to Panic in respect of this meeting of the government at Velepromet. First of all, there are no witnesses for the telephone conversation, and the Trial Chamber here decided to place its trust in Panic. Although this statement does not correspond to the statement by Witness Vujic, which -- or who did not confirm that Panic conveyed at the government meeting some sort of welcoming speech or Mrksic's agreement; however, in a small notebook, which is Exhibit 852, presented to the Trial Chamber, there is a note from the meeting in Velepromet, which took place allegedly on the 20th of November, 1991, which very briefly, in two or three sentences, allegedly records what happened. But the witness who actually took those notes, Panic, claims that the conclusions were adopted but that he did not actually record them in these two or three sentences, as if they were not important to him. Either they were not adopted or the whole event did not take place at all, and this is something that the Mrksic Defence asserts. It is interesting that this part of Panic's testimony and the conclusion of the Trial Chamber can be viewed through the transcript from page 14382 to 14384, where you can see clearly that Witness Panic, until 2001, takes the 21st of November, 1991, as the date that the meeting actually took place, but the position of the Defence is if Exhibit 852, the small notebook that I mentioned, were authentic and it was in the possession -- and had it been in the possession of Mr. Panic, he would not have been able to make such a crucial mistake because he could have used it to remind himself had his notes actually been made on the 21st of November, 1991. So the Defence, for the reasons stated above, believes that actually these notes were written sometime later. That is why, when we are considering this particular piece of evidence, we believe that the conclusions of the Trial Chamber, which arise from these assertions by Witness Panic, would not be taken by any reasonable trier of fact as evidence beyond any doubt. However, the fact that the war prisoners were not under the authority of Mile Mrksic can be seen from the order for the evacuation of the hospital. This is Exhibit 419, where the categories of persons that Mile Mrksic was authorised for are listed. So it is completely illogical that the Trial Chamber concluded that a part of an order for the same assignment was issued orally and a part was issued in writing because this is something that does not happen in practice. What is said in the order, which is Exhibit 419, is actually the assignment being issued by Mile Mrksic, and that is the evacuation of the wounded and sick persons from Vukovar Hospital and has nothing to do or does not refer to any treatment of prisoners of war. The security organs are in charge of taking care of prisoners of war, which can be seen from Exhibit 819, as well as from the fact that people for this operation were being sent by General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, who was at the time the chief of the Security Administration, and that the triage and evacuation of these persons headed by the group led by Witness Vujic is being conducted by this group, and this includes, also, the security organ, the security organs received from Belgrade, a list of members of the ZNG who were hiding at the hospital, and they also received an order to see or find out who these persons were and to detain them. What can Commander Mrksic have had to do with that, pursuant to the conclusions of the Trial Chamber? The organs of security communicated directly with General Aleksandar Vasiljevic from the hospital, and the buses from the hospital to the barracks were sent by Vujic and Sljivancanin, and nobody informed Mrksic about this because there was no need for that because he was not in charge of this category of persons. Besides the order on the evacuation of the patients from the hospital in the already-mentioned Exhibit 419, Mrksic again warned the town commanders about their duty to protect the security of property and persons in their areas of responsibility. So besides addressing all the commands before to apply the provisions of international humanitarian law and to establish town commands as commands that were in charge, Mrksic again now warned about the duty to protect property and persons at all places where military command was in power rather than civilian authority, and this order went out on the 20th of November, 1991. Such an order was also received by the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and he had to adhere to this order because besides his own unit, he also had 1.000 attached soldiers who happened to be in the Grabovo-Ovcara-Jakobovac sector. He also had a tank unit in Jakobovac, which was less than 1.000 metres away from Ovcara, and anti-aircraft guns and one tank who were located not far from the yellow house, just 200 metres from the hangar at Ovcara. You can see this location and the yellow house in photographs that are part of Exhibits 378 to 380. Witness P-014 arrived at the Command in the evening at around 2200 hours to see Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic with the request that the military police should not withdraw from the Ovcara Farm. (redacted)

You can continue now, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think that we are now ready to proceed, Mr. Vasic. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was speaking about the conclusion of the Trial Chamber from paragraph 625 that members of the TO can overrule members of the JNA. I consider that no reasonable trier of fact could come to such a conclusion when Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic himself claimed that there were no more than 40 members of the TO, and he had a force of several thousand men in his own unit and also armoured equipment in the immediate vicinity of the hangar. He also, as the commander of the 80th Brigade, had prepared his unit because as we have already said, he received an assignment on the 19th to prepare for guarding and securing prisoners of war. In the situation in which Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic said he found himself, he had to, as an experienced officer and commander, to refuse to hand over prisoners to anyone other than to the authorised powers. He should have guarded them or should have asked for reinforcements if he didn't have enough men, or to ask for buses and to transfer them to a different location. If he were to be ordered to hand them over to a TO unit, for example, he first had to make sure that the prisoners of war would not be in any danger, and he could have carried out the order under this condition only if he had received a written order and after inquiring in detail about the consequences of this order. Otherwise, he had to have refused the order and to address the immediately superior command. In any case, he had to use forces that he had at his disposal, and to throw out members of the TO from the hangar, and to prevent their further presence in his area of responsibility. Since Mrksic did not order anything - and this is what he said himself, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, I mean - he tried to interpret Mrksic's words. The duty of the commander -- of the town commander was clear, and Vojnovic was evidently aware of it, but he acted differently. Why he did this is something that the Trial Chamber did not establish. They accepted the testimony of this witness as one of the key witnesses to establish the guilt of Mile Mrksic. The Trial Chamber did not establish either why the list that was drafted of prisoners of war disappeared. These are the prisoners of war who were at the hangar on the 20th of November, 1991, and which ended up on the desk of the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, in the evening of that day. It's quite clear why this list was made; because this procedure was already applied in the case of prisoners of war at Mitnica who were at Ovcara from the 18th to the 19th of November, 1991, who were also guarded by the military police of the 80th Brigade. It is odd that despite the presence of these many members of the security services who were at Ovcara that day, as well as surprises from the Supreme Command and the Command of the 1st Military District, military and civilian investigators and forensic specialists who were carrying out their work pursuant to orders of the military court from Sid, how it happened that a large group of people disappeared, after coming around all the locations in the centre of Vukovar, this group of people disappeared, and this remained a secret for so many years. According to the findings of the Trial Chamber, this secret was created for reasons only known to himself by Colonel Mrksic, a commander of one brigade or, if you prefer, the temporary military force called "Operations Group South." If this is logical, acceptable, and if this is something that can be asserted beyond any reasonable doubt, is something for you to see. Somebody whose unit was sent to Vukovar overnight under such circumstances did not have the power or the authority to do what I mentioned earlier. This could not have been Mrksic because had he done that, on the following day he would have had to be arrested by the security organs whose task it is to discover the perpetrators of war crimes and other crimes. Therefore, Mrksic could not have given the order for security to withdraw from the Ovcara Farm, especially not through the security officer, Captain Karanfilov, and then make sure that all the JNA structures keep quiet about it. Why the Defence is convinced that Mile Mrksic did not issue the order on the withdrawal of the military police and on all the errors of the Trial Chamber in drawing conclusions, this is something that my colleague will address. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I move on to my part of the arguments, I wish to draw attention to an error in the transcript. On page 9, line 22, when referring to the exhibit my colleague Mr. Vasic mentioned, the exhibit number is erroneously recorded as "429," whereas it should be "419," And Exhibits 268 and 269 are not recorded in the transcript, but they were quoted by my colleague Mr. Vasic. Who issued the order of the withdrawal of the military police of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade and in what manner is one of the key facts in this case. Had such an order really been issued by Mile Mrksic, as the Trial Chamber erroneously concluded, not only would there have to be a written trace of this in the documents of Operations Group South and the reports to the higher command, but the order would also have had to include the manner of its implementation, that is, to whom and how the prisoners were to be handed over, as was the case with the prisoners from Mitnica only two days previously. As these were not ordinary prisoners of war but, rather, persons suspected of possible participation in war crimes and participants in a rebellion, as the military judiciary applying the then-valid legal provisions viewed these persons who were in conflict with the JNA, Mrksic did not have the right to decide on handing over these prisoners to anyone, nor was he authorised to do so. These prisoners as suspects, suspected of war crimes against the JNA, were within the purview of the security organs. Special teams consisting of high-ranking security officers were sent from the highest command in Belgrade to investigate, question, and prosecute prisoners suspected of perpetrating war crimes against the JNA. In addition to this, there was a clear order on prohibiting any exchange of all prisoners of war, which has not been challenged, and this certainly applied to these prisoners all the more so as they were suspected of perpetrating war crimes. The Trial Chamber failed to consider the possibility that if Captain Karanfilov really did issue such an order to Vezmarovic, such an order could only have arrived from the high security organs down the security chain of command or line of command, which had nothing to do with the line of command within the brigade and Commander Mrksic or the officers of the brigade. There is a completely separate issue, which is whether the 80th Motorised Brigade, which was in charge of guarding and securing these prisoners, was permitted on the basis of an oral order issued by a security officer to abandon the security of the hangar and withdraw the military police without any sort of hand-over of the prisoners. This is, of course, included in this appeal because in the view of the Defence the 80th Motorised Brigade was not authorised nor could it have withdrawn its military police from the hangar at Ovcara without a clear written order, and they should have done this following the procedure of listing and handing over the prisoners based on such an order. No reasonable trier of fact would accept this conclusion which was drawn by the Trial Chamber. Had Mrksic issued such an order before the briefing, this would certainly have been mentioned at the briefing, but no witness confirmed this, that such a thing happened. On the contrary, at the briefing, in addition to many other issues, the issue of security for the prisoners was discussed in view of the fact that they might have been under threat from the paramilitaries or civilians, but there was no mention of the fact that anyone, including Mrksic, had already issued an order on handing over the prisoners to anyone, including the TO, as the Court erroneously concluded. This same evidence excludes the possibility that Mrksic issued such an order during the briefing because not only has no Prosecution or Defence witness confirmed such a thing - I am referring to witnesses who were present at the briefing - but there is no mention of this in any written document, including the report from the briefing, the regular report from the briefing. Such an order issued by the commander would certainly have been recorded, and it would have been remembered by the participants in the briefing. Witness Vojnovic does not confirm this, either. Rather, he attempts by his own interpretation of words allegedly spoken by Mrksic and Mrksic's alleged actions, he tries to represent that such an order existed, but it's something that only he understood, allegedly understood. He at no point directly and simply asked his commander, Did you issue the order on the withdrawal of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and is that how I can understand your reply? Could any reasonable trier of fact accept the interpretation that an officer as experienced as Vojnovic was would make the decision -- such an important decision, as important as the decision on withdrawing his unit, and allegedly convey to his security officer, Vukosavljevic, without having received such an order directly from his commander, Mrksic, or asking him directly whether such an order existed. Mrksic's Defence wishes to point out that not only was Mrksic not allowed without an order from a superior command to decide on the fate of the prisoners and that he was not competent to do so, but that he had no reason whatsoever to do such a thing and allegedly hand over the prisoners to the local Territorial Defence because, as my colleague has already pointed out, not only was there no such order from the alleged government, but there was also no request issued by the so-called government either to the Command of Operations Group South or anyone else, and all this is the subject of a separate part of our appeal. Here, we wish to point out that the Trial Chamber failed to take into account the testimony of a very relevant witness, Witness Jaksic, who testified that he went to see Mrksic before this meeting in Velepromet and that Mrksic categorically refused to discuss the handing-over of the prisoners to anyone, including the Territorial Defence or the so-called civilian authorities or the so-called government, and it also failed to take into account his testimony as a participant in that session to the effect that this issue was not discussed at that session at all. The Trial Chamber concluded or established that after the second alleged meeting, Vojnovic and Mrksic were walking together, and Vojnovic came back and issued the order to Vukosavljevic, his security officer, to go to Ovcara and withdraw the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade. No reasonable trier of fact could have arrived at such a conclusion. First of all, there was no such second meeting. It is something that Witness Vojnovic and Vukosavljevic invented so that the responsibility for the withdrawal of Ovcara would fall on Mrksic rather than those who actually were responsible for this and who did this. First of all, it should be kept in mind what Vojnovic testified to in 1998 when not only was his memory much fresher and more objective, because at that time no one had yet been accused, including Mrksic, and this testimony before the military court in Novi Sad, when he testified about the arrival of an officer from the 80th Brigade who was immediately subordinated to Vojnovic, and he said that he came to see him at 2200 hours and spoke about Vezmarovic and Karanfilov. This indicates that in these proceedings, Vojnovic was not telling the truth when he stated that all this had been organised before 2000 hours. The time is very important here because the Defence believes that the time entered in the diary, 2235, is the correct time of the withdrawal of the military police and that the attempts of some witnesses whom the Trial Chamber relied on, who tried to represent this time as being a few hours earlier, is not correct. The Trial Chamber should have taken into account that Witness Vojnovic, in the course of his testimony before this Court, confessed that never before in the course of his testimonies did he mention that Vukosavljevic had been with him at the briefing on the 20th in the afternoon. His response to that was that he had forgotten that Vukosavljevic had been with him, but because he trusted Vukosavljevic, he testified to this fact before this Trial Chamber, although he did not remember it. But he accepted the fact because that's what Vukosavljevic claimed in his testimony, and they discussed this before their testimonies. So all this indicates that these two witnesses were in collusion before the testimony and they wanted their testimonies to corroborate each other when testifying before the Trial Chamber. This is also supported by other facts which these two witnesses tried to include in their testimony, and this will be discussed in another part of the appeal. In the meantime, in the Seselj case, the new testimony of Vojnovic completely --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: This will relate to the confidential motion and should not be dealt with at this stage. It's a matter Your Honours have already raised with counsel at the outset, and this should not be a subject of submissions, as I understand it. Anything from another case that has not been made part of a motion to admit within these proceedings is simply not on the record in these proceedings, and that's the end of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, what do you say about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I am referring to is the testimony of Witness Vojnovic before this Trial Chamber and not any other testimony, including the one in connection with Rule 115, so I'm now referring to the testimony before this Trial Chamber. I'm not touching on any of his statements that he gave later on in connection with 115. So Vojnovic in this case testified that before going to the briefing in Negoslavci, he sent Vukosavljevic to Ovcara to look at the situation, as he said, and Vukosavljevic in these proceedings testified that in Negoslavci, in front of the room where the briefing was held, he waited for as long as an hour and a half, and this excludes one or the other, especially bearing in mind Vojnovic's testimony before this Chamber that he was late to the meeting, and it says: "However, I was late to that meeting, and by the time I arrived, the other officers were leaving already."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, I see you have no further problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. Despite the clear record in the transcript of the reference to the Seselj case, it appears that Mr. Domazet does not intend to refer to the Seselj case, and of course, I have no objections to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Domazet, you can proceed, and you know what are the rules with which you have to abide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not touching upon the testimony in the case mentioned. If that's how it was, Vojnovic could not have sent Vukosavljevic to Ovcara in such a brief space of time, nor could he have come back and waited for an hour and a half, because during that time Vojnovic spent some 15 or 20 minutes at the most in the briefing room because as he himself said, it all lasted a very short time. Because of this, we consider that this alleged encounter of all three is invented, Mrksic, Vukosavljevic, and Vojnovic after the briefing, and the testimony of a relevant witness, Gluscevic, completely excludes this possibility, and not only his testimony, but other testimonies as well. Vojnovic, who did not remember at all that Vukosavljevic had been in Negoslavci during the briefing as he himself said before the Court, as he trusted Vukosavljevic, he not only remembered this later on but also this meeting of the three of them. Had this meeting really taken place, Vojnovic would have remembered it well and testified about it before and not only at this trial after he had heard Witness Vukosavljevic say that he had been at Negoslavci with him on that occasion. Vojnovic testified that at the briefing, he spoke about the threat to the prisoners, and admitted that he didn't even mention that a security officer, that is, Vukasinovic, the security officer of the Guards Brigade, was there. This is inexplicable. Also, when asked by the Defence, he testified that while he was there, the prisoners were separated by a rope and were not under any physical threat. This also indicates that the testimony -- the present testimony before this Trial Chamber was adjusted after him being in collusion with Vukosavljevic and some others. When asked by the Defence before this Trial Chamber, whether before the investigating judge of the Special Court in Belgrade, Albric [phoen], he told him that Mrksic had said that he had other obligations and that he did not issue any orders regarding the situation at Ovcara. He responded, I quote the words from the record in this trial: [In English] "No, he didn't say that to me. He said that" -- "he said that to Drago Vukosavljevic. To me, he said, 'Don't tell me anything about it.' He didn't do anything else." [Interpretation] Vojnovic then asserts that he didn't hear something like this from Mrksic, and in some way he transfers this to Vukosavljevic, and Vukosavljevic claims something completely the opposite in his testimony. He says that allegedly Mrksic and Vojnovic went to one side, spoke for a few minutes without his presence, and then Mrksic went off in another direction, and Vukosavljevic approached Vojnovic and told him to go to Ovcara and convey his order on the withdrawal of that unit. For the record, my colleague says it's not entered in the record. Before the judge of the special court, he said that Mrksic did not issue any order to him regarding the situation at Ovcara. No reasonable trier of fact could have concluded on the basis of such testimonies that Mrksic issued the order on the withdrawal of the military police of the JNA from Ovcara. If we take into account the testimony of Witness Trifunovic, a witness relied on by the Trial Chamber, that not only did he not remember that he saw Vojnovic at the briefing or immediately after, and this was the witness who took the minutes, but Witness Trifunovic, and this is especially important, remembers that Vojnovic did arrive, but much later after the briefing, looking for Mrksic, who was then absent, although according to Trifunovic's testimony, it follows that Vojnovic did not find Mrksic there. Evidently, this is not about the alleged meeting at the end of the briefing and this meeting never took place, but Witness Vojnovic came much later that evening looking for Mrksic and evidently failed to find him there, certainly because Mrksic had then already left Belgrade. And it's interesting that Vojnovic didn't testify to that at all or mention it in his testimony. Only -- well, why he didn't do so, we can only assume that he wished to conceal something, and when he failed to find Mrksic, he spoke to someone else. With respect to Witness Trifunovic, one of the witnesses the Trial Chamber relied on, although it did not believe him only when he correctly stated, and he was the one who made the minutes, that the briefings were held at 5.00 p.m. and not later, as the Trial Chamber concluded, and that reports were sent to the higher command usually at 6.00 p.m. The Court believes this witness in respect of some other facts, too, that he obviously misstated completely. The Defence actually believes that he lied on purpose in order to remove responsibility from some others and to pin it on Mrksic, who was already facing the Court, and it's not only on the basis of his personal observations; rather, he refers to transcript 8138 and the war diary. He says that Mrksic went to Belgrade on the morning of the 21st. The Defence believes that this is not an error in terms of the entry made; rather, this is an ill-intentioned entry that is erroneous and that was made by this witness. He knows full well who made and signed the order of the 21st at 6.00. This is transcript Reference 8138, and he testified that he did not recognise Mrksic's signature. It is not only that this is not Mrksic's signature and order because this order was made and signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Panic; rather, this is a forgery and an attempt to hide or conceal something through this order. That is why the witness tries to prove, as it were, that he claims, as the one and only witness to do so, that Mrksic, as a matter of fact, was in Negoslavci around midnight. In this way, he is certainly helping the person who was standing in for the absent commander to enter this forged order at 6.00 in the morning, however, without Mrksic's signature because quite simply he was not there, and then intentionally he makes the wrong entry because Mrksic left for Belgrade by helicopter. Unfortunately, Witness Trifunovic, together with those who participated in this, managed with this false testimony to deceive even the Trial Chamber and to channel the blame for the fate of the prisoners at Ovcara to Mrksic rather than to have those who were the only ones who could do this after Commander Mrksic went to Belgrade shoulder the blame, and he went to Belgrade on the 20th of November, 1991. In order to amplify this invented story of his before the Court, he even invents a meeting at midnight that night, and he testifies, transcript Reference 8168: "I later heard that Colonel Mrksic returned just before midnight." It's not only that he's the only witness who says that and that this is in total contravention of the testimony of many Defence witnesses, but it is inexplicable where it is that Mrksic returned from, and if Mrksic was in Negoslavci that night, why did he not personally sign, the following morning at 6.00, the order that was entered in the diary, and that is quite controversial anyway, as already stated, and if he went to Belgrade only at 8.15, which was also misstated in the war diary? Perhaps the motive of the this witness can be seen or at least gleaned - transcript Reference 8168 - when, in response to the Prosecutor's question as to where Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was, he testifies that on the 18th -- where Panic was on the 18th and 19th, but in response to the direct question of the Prosecutor: "And what about the 20th?" [In English] "Even you didn't make note about it. Do you know where he was on 20? Can you say or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't, I don't know." [Interpretation] It is impossible that he cannot and that he does not know where he was, especially when Mrksic was not in Negoslavci. Obviously, it is not a question of him not being able to or, rather -- simply, it is a question of him not wanting to know that Panic made the order and signed it on that morning. It is impossible that this witness does not know where Lieutenant-Colonel Panic is, his immediate superior, especially not that night when he witnessed Panic in the absence of Mrksic was commander of the entire Operations Group South. These are the untruths made by -- stated by this witness that were regrettably accepted by the Trial Chamber and that are in total contravention of the adduced evidence made in detail with regard to Mrksic's depart to Belgrade, and no reasonable trier of fact would not accept this. Obviously, this testimony by Trifunovic had, as its objective, to deny the evidence that Mrksic on that evening of the 20th after the briefing went to Belgrade with Colonel Coric by car. The Defence analysed the evidence in its appeal, especially the testimony of Colonel Coric, the former commander of the Guards Brigade who, on that evening and in agreement with Mrksic, waited for him to complete the briefing and go to Belgrade; and then there was also the testimony of Mrs. Mrksic, Mrksic's wife, who says that his sister arrived from -- arrived in Belgrade that evening, and she arrived with a group of refugees from Borovo Naselje, and she was supposed to organise her arrival; and finally the testimony of driver Renicje [phoen], who went to pick up Mrksic's sister and brought her to Mrksic's apartment that same evening, talked to him, and later on the following morning he came to pick Mrksic up at his apartment, and he drove him to the Command of the Guards Brigade in Belgrade, as previously agreed, and then he went to meet the helicopter from Negoslavci on which Major Tesic arrived, and then he drove both of them to a reception hosted by the State Secretary of National Defence, which is why he actually came to Belgrade. In contravention of this clear and unequivocal testimony, it is only Witness Trifunovic who testifies and who incorrectly or intentionally falsifies the entry in the war diary, tries to portray things as if Mrksic went to Belgrade only on the following day. In the sixth ground, the Defence analysed this false testimony of Witness Trifunovic, who, truth to tell, does not testify to having seen any of this personally, the departure by helicopter, et cetera, but he testifies on the basis of what he saw in the war diary, and it's obvious why. Another lie that he stated was that he allegedly worked on some map that night and that Colonel Pavkovic helped him in that. In these proceedings, it was established that Colonel Pavkovic was in Sremska Mitrovica that night and that he was engaged in a completely different task, so this is yet another untruth stated by this witness, and in this way he was trying somehow establish that Mrksic was in Negoslavci that night. Why? We can understand why, I believe. On the other hand, it is stated that a group of officers went by helicopter with Mr. Mrksic, but it was only Tesic who went on that morning helicopter to Belgrade. Mrksic had done that the previous night. The Trial Chamber establishes that Mrksic's intention was not to have the JNA hand over the prisoners of war to any other Serbian army, and that is paragraph 610. This is a correct conclusion on the part of the Trial Chamber, and later on the Trial Chamber changed that when they established that at one point, Mrksic changed this decision of his. Mrksic never changed his decision, and he never ordered that the prisoners be handed over to any Serb military unit. The Trial Chamber comes to this conclusion because they take into account and recognise part of Panic's testimony, Panic being his deputy, about this night between the 20th and 21st, and his false testimony that this was allegedly discussed at the meeting of the so-called government in Velepromet, and that what was stated was that prisoners of war should be handed over to the civilian organs. The Trial Chamber established that Mrksic ordered that the POWs be handed over to -- sent to the barracks. That is not true. Sljivancanin himself says that he personally ordered that from the hospital, the buses should go to the barracks of the JNA, and also what should be borne in mind is that Mrksic had the order to carry out an evacuation at the hospital and did not consist only of the evacuation of the prisoners of war but primarily of the ill and wounded. Major Sljivancanin, according to the security chain and the tasks that he got from the Security Administration of the JNA, rather, his superiors, on the basis of this chain, not only had the task that was related to prisoners of war -- I do apologise, but I have to repeat this because this is important. I see that my -- my colleague says that this is recorded differently in the transcript. We claim that Mrksic had an order to have the evacuation at the hospital carried out, that is to say, to have the sick and wounded evacuated from the hospital, and all of those who are there, and that the security organs were in charge of establishing who is not a sick or wounded person, who was infiltrated, and who had simply changed their clothing and were in the hospital and who were possible war crimes suspects, and that was precisely done in the hospital, and this does not pertain to authority or orders of Mile Mrksic. Otherwise, Major Sljivancanin, as he testified himself, ordered that the buses stop at the JNA barracks, and he did not ask Mrksic for his approval, and he had no need to do that, and he did not inform him about that. It is not only -- it is not only that he did not inform him about that throughout that day, which was only logical because he was engaged in work that was not carried out on the basis of orders of Mrksic; rather, it was along the security chain, and these are -- and this had to do with potential war crimes suspects and their selection at the hospital. This is obvious from the testimony before the Court that while Colonel Vujic and Major Sljivancanin were in the hospital, they had this dilemma what to do. They did not call Colonel Mrksic; rather, they called General Aleksandar Vasiljevic and General Tumanov, who were their superiors along the security chain. The conclusion is, on the basis of this kind of evidence, no reasonable trier of fact could establish that Mile Mrksic had issued an order on the withdrawal of the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade from the hangar at Ovcara or that the withdrawal took place at any other time but 2235 hours as was precisely recorded in the diary of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, and I would like to proceed from this point where my colleague stopped, with your permission. We have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes, you have ten minutes, and I think it would be useful if you would devote part of the time available to you summarise this argument that has been made, but ten minutes altogether, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to use two or three minutes to deal with aiding and abetting and inhuman treatment that our client was found guilty of, and this is based on what is stated in paragraph 308 through 316 of the judgement, that Panic, Vojnovic, Vukasinovic, and Vukosavljevic informed Mrksic about what happened that afternoon at Ovcara and that there was no reaction to these reports. First of all, as regards the content of what Panic conveyed to Mrksic in his own words, one may conclude that he had said that the situation was under control, but Vojnovic should be consulted in terms of whether he could provide for the security of the prisoners of war. The credibility of this witness has already been discussed, and I would just like to point out here that this witness cannot be a reliable one in relation to any statement, including this one. However, after 1600 hours in the war diary of the 80th motorised -- sorry, the operations diary of the 80th Motorised Brigade, there is an order on the reinforcement of the security of the Ovcara Farm, so there was a reaction after all. As for what Witness Vukasinovic said to Mrksic, that happened after 1700 hours, according to what Vukasinovic said, because he first got some rest and then he reported to Mrksic, which is to say that there was nothing urgent going on, and since security had already been reinforced, Mrksic said to him that he could go. As for what Vojnovic conveyed about what had happened that afternoon, Mr. Domazet referred to that in part, and also, you can partly see that from the testimony of those who attended the briefing who do not remember that Vojnovic referred to anything urgent, anything critical, and he could not have made any such references because he left Ovcara when there was full order there and control of the military police of his unit. After the briefing, we heard testimony that Mrksic called the commanders of the APC Company and told him to be available if necessary for securing the prisoners of war. So this all shows all the things that Mrksic did before he went to Belgrade on the evening of the 20th of November, 1991. Mrksic cannot be responsible because had he ordered what the Trial Chamber found, he would have ordered that down the chain of command, and that would have been a normal thing. However, this order went down the security chain. It is not logical that Mrksic issued this order, and he did not have any authority for that kind of thing. Therefore, there is no omission in what he did, as found by the Trial Chamber, and he cannot be responsible for aiding and abetting in torture and inhumane treatment as found by the Trial Chamber. For that reason, on all counts that he was pronounced guilty, we propose that Mile Mrksic be declared not responsible because there are no elements that beyond a reasonable doubt prove that they're elements for which he was sentenced. As for the sentence, we believe that the Trial Chamber did not take into account all the mitigating circumstances when they passed this sentence, first of all, for the acts of aiding and abetting, and that the sentence is too severe. Mrksic did not have any authority or any duties for the triage, transport, or the security of the prisoners of war. In the time that I have left, I would just like to move to private session, Your Honours, because I would like to address one more issue in two or three sentences that was the topic of the appeal, but it relates to a protected witness, and for that reason I left it for the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Registrar, we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session is, of course, finished. We are going into public session, and I will repeat that, in fact, the Defence for Mr. Mrksic has completed its task for this morning, and we will now have a 15-minute pause. The Court will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. So it's you, Mr. Rogers, now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So please start your hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm grateful. Your Honours, I have very much in mind the comments that you made at the outset of the hearing today relating to not wanting to hear again the submissions that are set out within our brief, and I'm also very mindful that this is not a rehearing, although Your Honours may be forgiving for having -- listening to the submissions from opposing counsel that this was, in fact, a re-hearing. The primary thrust of my early submissions this morning is that most if not all of that you have heard from counsel representing Mr. Mrksic has already been advanced, has been heard, tried - literally - tested, and regrettably for Mr. Mrksic, rejected, and the function of this Tribunal and this Chamber, of course, is not to revisit that unless good cause and good reason can be demonstrated. Your Honours, we've responded at length to Mr. Mrksic's appeal in our response brief, to many if not all of the points that he has raised, as he appears to really have just gone through them again, and I'm not going to repeat those. The order of our submissions will be this: First, I'll provide a short overview. Then my co-counsel, Mr. Wood and Ms. Lewis, will address some specific issues relating to Mrksic's appeal, which we had identified to be those which were primarily advanced by counsel for Mr. Mrksic, that is the withdrawal order, and to a lesser extent perhaps the security line of command. Those will address Grounds 6, 7 and 8. Mr. Wood will deal with those relating to Mr. Mrksic's role in the order to withdraw, and Ms. Lewis will briefly address Grounds 1, 2, 3, and 8 relating to the role of the 80th and local commands' security organs. Your Honours, just, then, to turn to my overview, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber reasonably and properly convicted Mile Mrksic of aiding and abetting the murders of 194 protected prisoners of war, many of whom were sick and wounded, when he ordered the withdrawal of the 80th Motorised Brigade, the only protective force keeping the killers at bay. In addition, they properly and reasonably convicted Mile Mrksic of aiding and abetting the torture and cruel treatment of those prisoners. These convictions were based on his failure to prevent the severe beatings and appalling conditions of their detention during the afternoon and evening of the 20th of November, 1991, until their eventual slaughter. The Trial Chamber found, at judgement pages 627 and 628 -- paragraph 627 and 628 that his failures to act rendered both practical assistance and encouragement to those at Ovcara seeking revenge --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Slow down. Both practical assistance and encouragement to those at Ovcara seeking revenge on those unfortunate individuals. Your Honours, in order to understand Mile Mrksic's position of authority, it is perhaps helpful to understand at the outset how Operation Group South was organised. Your Honours, I've produced a small Powerpoint -- I hope it won't be death by Powerpoint, but a short Powerpoint setting out the structure. The first slide, which I hope is on your screens now, shows at the top "Operation Group South" and we've put in there the Guards Motorised Brigade, the reason being that the command structure for the relevant period of this indictment -- of the Guards Brigade and Operation Group South was the same, Mile Mrksic being the commander and Lieutenant-Colonel Panic being the Chief of Staff. Do Your Honours have it on your screens? Yes. The appointment of Mrksic was on the 8th of October, 1991, as commander of Operational Group South, trial judgement paragraph 70, and the significance is that all units serving in that zone of responsibility were under his and the GMTBR's de jure command. Originally, the Vukovar Hospital was under Operational Group North, but on the 18th of November, and in our submission, a mark of the respect with which Mr. Mrksic must have been held, the taking of that hospital was put into his zone of responsibility, Operational Group South, and he was ordered to take the hospital. Within the command structure of the Guards Motorised Brigade was, of course, the security organ structure, and you'll see that the chief of security for the Guards Motorised Brigade was Veselin Sljivancanin. Therefore, because he -- they also formed the command structure of OG South, he was also in that position of responsibility. His deputy was Major Vukasinovic, and also, he had within that structure a security officer, Captain Karanfilov. Your Honours, I mention those names in order to just identify who they are and where they sit. The other security organs from other chains of command, the Trial Chamber found, would also be subordinate to him; so, for example, the 80th Motorised Brigade. That's trial judgement 127. They also, security organs, had their own chain of command in respect of counter-intelligence assignments, and that is what has been alluded to by the Defence. I'll turn to that briefly later on. Ms. Lewis will develop it. That's trial judgement 127. Then for completeness, also within Operational Group South and subordinated to it was the 80th Motorised Brigade, trial judgement 274, and you'll see that the 80th has one company of military police under the command of Captain Dragan Vezmarovic. Also, it has its own security organ, Captain Vukosavljevic. Unusually, the Guards Motorised Brigade also had two battalions of MPs at its disposal. I haven't shown them on there because they're distracting, but unlike the 80th, which only had a company maybe of 100 -- 60 to 100 men, the Guards had two whole battalions, something like 4 to 5 times in each battalion the number available within the 80th Motorised Brigade. Your Honours, if I provided sufficient information with the slide, I'll take it off the screen, if I may, so it doesn't become a distraction, and proceed with my submissions. Your Honour, to turn to our main argument, listening to the submissions of Mr. Mrksic, essentially what he says is that the Trial Chamber's conclusion was based upon an argument that, Who was it if it was not him? In our submission, the effects of his arguments before this Appeals Chamber is really to assert the complete reverse, which is that it was anyone but him that was responsible for what happened. That is, despite him being the commander of the Motorised Brigade, as the Trial Chamber found: A, if not the premier unit of the JNA, trial judgement paragraph 61, commander of the Operational Group placed in charge of the politically sensitive evacuation of the civilian prisoners of war from the Vukovar Hospital, such evacuation being carried out as it was in the eyes of the International Community and media, in the presence of European monitors, the International Committee of the Red Cross, high-ranking diplomats and many others, and despite the reliable evidence of his continual involvement in the decision-making process relating to the custody of the prisoners throughout the 19th and 20th of November, 1991. Despite all this, he asserts that he was not responsible for the care, security, or ultimately the deaths of those prisoners in any way. This, he argues, was the responsibility of others. In making his arguments, as is apparent from the submissions that you've heard this morning, Mrksic consistently criticises the Trial Chamber's approach to its decision-making by citing to other evidence in the record, suggesting other conclusions should have been drawn from it. He attacks the credibility of witnesses and exhibits, points to other evidence and exhibits from which he says other conclusions could have been drawn. But as Your Honours will appreciate, these submissions fundamentally fail to understand the nature of these proceedings in this Chamber. As you have already said, this is not a hearing de novo, nor is it an opportunity to repeat again that which has already been said at trial. In order to unseat the Trial Chamber's conclusions on the facts in this case, and its assessment of the evidence, the appellant must demonstrate that the factual conclusions reached by the Trial Chamber, as Your Honours know, were ones that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached when assessing the totality of the evidence. Of course, the Defence would -- they must attack individual pieces, but the Trial Chamber very much had in mind those individual attacks. It took them into account, and it looked at the whole picture. The standards to be applied relate to both findings based on direct evidence and such circumstantial evidence. Your Honours have recently pronounced that again in the Martic appeal judgement at paragraph 11, the footnote 23 there citing to the many other cases in which that has already been established: Strugar, Hadzihasanovic, Blagojevic, amongst many others. So in this case, in relation to the circumstantial inference that Mrksic must have ordered the withdrawal of the 80th Motorised Brigade from Ovcara, it is our submission that the factual findings from which that inference is drawn are left intact, as Mrksic cannot show that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have made those individual findings, and thus, he fails to show that the inference is one no reasonable Trial Chamber could have drawn from the facts it found to exist. In reaching its careful conclusions about this incident, which itself only lasted two to three days, the Trial Chamber was entrusted with the heaviest of responsibilities facing a decision-maker, that is, to determine the criminal responsibility of the appellant. In doing so, it weighed, sifted, reflected upon, and it's quite clear it did, and assessed 188 days of oral testimony over this short 2- to 3-day time frame. 84 witnesses gave live evidence. It considered 885 exhibits in various forms: photographic, film, paper, and written statements. It considered much of what my friends point to. For example, they refer, in one of the few direct references during the course of their submissions, to any testimony, exhibit, or trial judgement paragraph. They do refer to Trifunovic at transcript 8168 as a snippet, but the Trial Chamber considered it, and they footnoted it at Footnote 1289 in the judgement, just showing how carefully they considered the evidence in this case. He referred also to the differences between Vukosavljevic and Vojnovic regarding the events at the briefing. At length, they were developed before you as they were developed before the Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber respecting that devoted six pages to assessing the evidence relating to what occurred around that time; paragraphs 309 to 322. Every appellate court that does not conduct de novo hearings, as this one does not, recognises that it cannot hope to perform again that task which has been given to the Trial Chamber. What it can do is supervise the decision-making process, but in so doing, properly recognises the need to accord great deference to the actual fact-finding tribunal, and we submit particularly in a case such as this, where there was a lot of evidence to go through, that deference should be great because the Trial Chamber was in a position to assess the witnesses live, their demeanour, and ultimately their believability, and particularly in this case where so much of the evidence that was given was live oral testimony. It's not a case like it's a paper case, and Your Honours may have some experience of trying fraud cases where perhaps you don't hear many witnesses. You just look at mounds and mounds of paper. Perhaps the same arguments can't be made about the assessment of demeanour, believability, hearing the witnesses live. That's not the case here. And as can be recognised in this Chamber - Tadic Appeal Judgement 64 - different decision-makers can reasonably reach opposite conclusions upon the same totality of the evidence. This shows that the mere fact other evidence exists which could create a different conclusion will not mean that the conviction is wrong. What matters is how the Trial Chamber assessed the evidence. In this case, as a matter of law and in fact, the appellant has failed to show any error on the part of the Trial Chamber in how it assessed the evidence of witnesses or generally. The Trial Chamber was very careful to express how it was going to assess the evidence; trial judgement 11 to 16. It recognised that there were conflicts and that it would need to resolve some but not all of them. When it assessed witnesses, it gave explanations as to why it accepted or rejected them. For example, in relation to the Chief of Staff, Deputy Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Panic at trial judgement 297, it said this: "The Chamber notes that it has reviews the evidence of Panic with great care, especially about the relevant events of the 19th and 20th of November, 1991, and has considered it in the light of the other evidence about these events. It has also carefully weighed its assessment of the credibility of Panic, taking into account his demeanour as he gave evidence, the events that are otherwise established to have occurred, and the demeanour of those who gave differing accounts about these events." In the Chamber's assessment, Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was generally and in respect of most matters, an honest and reliable witness. Compare that with the assertion of the Defence in this case that they found his statement was in most part not believable. That's not right. Another example, and I give a few, in relation to the witness Susic at trial judgement 299 to 302, the Chamber devoted two and a half pages of its judgement in recounting the concerns of the Defence, addressing them, assessing the competing witness testimony, and reaching its conclusions. In relation to the witness Vojnovic at trial judgement 321, they said this: "The circumstances as disclosed by the evidence leave the issue as contentious and unresolved. Because of this, the Chamber approaches the evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic with extreme caution. The Chamber observes, however, that when dealing with this issue, Vojnovic gave a clear impression of being frank and honest in respect of the questioning of reporting to Mile Mrksic as best his recollection of the interviews and proceedings in 1998 allowed." Other examples - and I will stop here - in relation to a conflict between Vujic and the witness Korica at trial judgement 173, the Trial Chamber again weighed, balanced, concluded, and gave reasons why it preferred evidence where it did reject accounts or even partial accounts of an individual witness. In our respectful submission, therefore, it is very clear that this Trial Chamber had very much in its collective mind the need to weigh and assess the witnesses very carefully and to reach a proper considered decision in relation to their individual reliability when necessary. It didn't do it in every case, nor did it need to do so in every case, but what is clear from their overall approach is how they dealt with this assessment, and insofar as his challenges relate to the Trial Chamber's approach to the assessment of evidence, therefore, and most of them do, if not all, the way they are framed, his challenges must fail. Mrksic seeks to blame in this case the local commands or the Command of the 80th Motorised Brigade or the security organs for what happened. In relation to the 80th, he refers to an exhibit, although he doesn't give the exhibit reference, the 19th of November, which he says shows they were expecting prisoners the next day. In our submission, it doesn't show that. It shows that there was a discussion at the briefing relating to the evacuation of the hospital but not about where prisoners were going or who was to receive them. That was because, of course, that hadn't been decided on the 18th-19th. So he seeks to create doubt about who it was that made the order to withdraw. The Trial Chamber didn't consider there was any reasonable doubt about that. He doesn't dispute that he was the overall commander of Operational Group South. He doesn't dispute that the hospital evacuation was within his zone of responsibility. He doesn't dispute that he ordered it. Instead, he seeks to confine his responsibility, you may think confusingly, to simply the evacuation of civilians, hospital workers, sick and wounded, and more, that that was delegated to Veselin Sljivancanin. That's at paragraph 139 of his appeal brief. He argues that Sljivancanin was delegated to do this because the Security Administration was in charge of the evacuation of prisoners of war and their security, and so he says he had no responsibility over that. And he refers, Your Honours, in oral submissions to Exhibit 819, which he relies upon to say that the security organ was in charge. Well, Your Honours, in our submission, if you look at Exhibit 819, which is a report dated the 12th of October, 1991, so many days before, from the security organ of the GMTBR, what it refers to is the assessment of security issues, the interviewing of suspects, and in which -- in the body of the report the details of what have been carried out is set out. It doesn't refer to the security of prisoners of war, only to their interview. That's consistent with the triage that carried out -- that was carried out. And interestingly, right at the very end, the author of the report says this: "The security organs are under great strain because they're performing many tasks which do not fall under their jurisdiction." In this case, the order to evacuate the hospital and to deal with the prisoners of war came from Mile Mrksic, that the security of those prisoners would not normally come, in our submission, within the jurisdiction of the Security Administration. That would be a matter for Mrksic, which is why Sljivancanin was tasked with the whole thing by him, as the Trial Chamber found. So, Your Honour, he argues that the obvious choice to cover the civilian aspects was Sljivancanin, and I've explained why it's, in fact, the other way around. And so he says the movement of the prisoners was nothing to do with him. Whatever happened to them was down to others, particularly Sljivancanin and the security organs; Appeal Brief 140 to 149. He also alleges that the crimes occurred in the zone of responsibility of the 80th and suggests that because Mrksic had created local commands, somehow they were responsible for what happened; Appeal Briefs 25 to 102. But the Trial Chamber largely relied upon, and correctly, in our submission, the evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, his Chief of Staff, when it found that the 80th Motarised Brigade came to be at Ovcara on Mrksic's orders - trial judgement 305 - and this was because there had been an interim decision by Mile Mrksic as to what should be done regarding the transport of prisoners - trial judgement 305 - following on from the government meeting. Interestingly, Mrksic, in his appeal brief at 167, himself states that Panic's role was "a deputy commander." Well, yes, we agree. He then goes on to say this: "He was in charge of supervising and providing the implementation of commanders' orders. His role should be viewed in that light." The Trial Chamber did consider Panic's role in that light, and thus, it's no surprise, in our submission, that in the implementation of Mrksic's various orders concerning the prisoners, Lieutenant-Colonel Panic regularly appears. We see him present at the government meeting - trial judgement 225, 296, and 305 - where the fate of the prisoners was discussed.
