He's at the barracks of the JNA on the morning of the 20th, where the prisoners were being held and mistreated - trial judgement 296 - and later again, he turns up at Ovcara to where they were transferred, beaten, and ultimately murdered; trial judgement 308. At all points, Mrksic received reports from Panic as to his observations and recommendations. He's reporting from the barracks; he's reporting from the government session; he's reporting from Ovcara, where he sets out what it is he has seen. Why should that happen if it is not Mrksic that is responsible? In addition, it's clear that Mrksic ordered Sljivancanin to carry out the actual evacuation and deliver their prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica; trial judgement 191 and 295. The roles of these two men is not mutually exclusive. They simply reflect different aspects of what was going on that day with Mrksic retaining overall responsibility. The trial judgement found that Panic reported his observations of the scenes at Ovcara to Mile Mrksic - trial judgement 308 - and in his evidence at transcript Reference 14473, Panic says this, relating to what it is he reported: "I conveyed that they needed to check the security detail and reinforce it, and I said that I thought that somebody ought to be sent there whose specialty it was so that they could make appropriate corrections, and I concluded the same with Vojnovic; namely, that security needed to be reinforced. "Q. And you state in paragraph 86, this is in reference to the statement: 'As part of that that told Mrksic that you had doubts about the safety of those prisoners at Ovcara?' "A. Yes. "Q. And you wanted someone to evaluate the situation' - if you look at page 87 - 'to make sure that the safety of the prisoners was guaranteed.' Those are your words? Paragraph 87. "A. Yes." And then he goes on at page 14474 to offer his view as to explaining why he'd said what he'd said. He said this: "Considering my feelings about the local Serbian TO and the fact that Colonel Mrksic knew about the threat to the safety of the prisoners posed by the local TO, he could have used units of the Guards Motorised Brigade to neutralise or eliminate this threat. The local Serbian TO was no match for the Guards Motorised Brigade." And it was put to him, is that what he'd said in his previous statement. He said yes. "Is that what you said?" "Yes." Your Honour, in relation to Sljivancanin, the Prosecution adopts its submissions concerning his role that it has made in its own appeal and in response to Sljivancanin's appeal, and I don't intend to repeat those submissions within Mrksic's appeal. Mrksic was the ultimate decision-maker, in our submission, on the fate of the prisoners, at least in Operational Group South's zone of responsibility. It's interesting that Defence quote to what Jaksic -- the Defence witness Jaksic. The Defence's own witness, Jaksic, who was previously the commander of the TO before he was -- local TO before he was replaced by Mrksic, in fact, Jaksic said that he was asked on the morning of the 20th of November by the so-called government to act as a mediator - that's his word, "mediator" - between the government and Mile Mrksic on that morning, and he says at transcript 11920 that it was to Mrksic he went to ask if the prisoners, on behalf of the government, could stay in the area, that is, not to be removed out to Sremska Mitrovica, to be told firmly, No, they're going to Sremska Mitrovica. Your Honours, in our respectful submission, what is relevant about that is that the local people, those in the know, as it were, those who could be expected to know to whom it was they had to go to get a decision, were not going to Veselin Sljivancanin or the security line of administration to make this vital decision; they were going to Mile Mrksic on the morning of the 20th of November. Why would that be, if the truth was he had no responsibility? Mrksic was informed about and made decisions relating to the care of the prisoners that day on the 20th. He knew about the incidents at the barracks. Susic and Panic told him - trial judgement 301 - and the Trial Chamber found that these were incidents that Mile Mrksic would have been told about because this was an issue, quote, "in which he had a very direct concern and responsibility, just as he had a direct concern and responsibility as to what should be done with the prisoners that day." It was he that decided to divert the prisoners to Ovcara, he that ordered the 80th to receive the prisoners at Ovcara. He knew that the problems at Ovcara, and he chose to do nothing about them, then or later, in our submission. When he did act, it was to withdraw the only security they had and to consign them to their fate. The presence of those prisoners and the political situation regarding their treatment was in the forefront of the international mind at the time. Delegations were being regularly received at Mrksic's command post. Why would it be there if it was another that was responsible? And in our submission, it is absurd to suggest that the only concern Mrksic had was for civilians and that somehow the prisoners within his zone of responsibility were actually outside of his concern within that zone of responsibility. He was the commander entrusted with the taking of the hospital and its subsequent evacuation. It was to him as commander that others turned to assistance be decisions about the movement of prisoners and their security, and in our submission it is absurd, again, to suggest that he would not have been involved in this process, given the sensitivities at the time, the clear need for authority at the time, or that anyone but him, in such a sensitive situation, could or would have ordered the withdrawal of the 80th Motorised Brigade MPs. The Defence have posited the question: "Well, surely he wouldn't have done such a thing because others within the JNA chains of command would have been alarmed at such an activity." But, Your Honours, that doesn't reflect what may be the reality here, that others should also have been before a tribunal, facing up to their criminal responsibilities for what occurred. Your Honours, and the Court below were only trying these defendants, and it may not have been able to answer precisely why things happened. There are not always answers to everything, but in this case, having sifted and weighed all of the evidence, the Trial Chamber was satisfied that Mile Mrksic's criminal responsibility was established in this case, and in our submission, the Trial Chamber's findings are both logical and unassailable, and his appeal should be dismissed. Your Honours, what I propose now to do is to hand over to Mr. Wood to develop the submissions in relation to the order to withdraw, unless there are any questions for me at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Great. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the heart of Mile Mrksic's conviction for aiding and abetting the murders of 194 people is the finding that he ordered the withdrawal of the military police from Ovcara Farm on 20 November 1991. As Your Honours are aware, the Chamber concluded that Colonel Mrksic ordered the Military Police Company of the 80th Motorised Brigade to leave Ovcara that evening, an act which delivered the Vukovar Hospital prisoners into the hands of the 300 murderous paramilitaries and TO members who had gathered there. The Chamber concluded that Mrksic knew this act would likely result in the murders of these men and women. Mrksic has failed in his Grounds 6, 7 and 8 of his appeal to show that this conclusion was one that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have made, and his appeal should be dismissed. Over the course of the next few minutes, I'll highlight the key findings that the Trial Chamber made as it picked its way through this extensive trial record to conclude that it was Mrksic who gave that order. I'll walk the Appeals Chamber through the Trial Chamber's significant findings to highlight the precision of the Trial Chamber's analysis and to show that this finding was the only reasonable conclusion available from the evidence. Now, I'll start by building a little bit on what you've just heard about the background of Mile Mrksic and his position and role in the events of 19 and 20 November 1991. The Chamber found that Mrksic was the key military commander in relation to the Vukovar Hospital evacuation. A wealth of evidence showed that Mrksic was the man to whom all authorities turned when it came time for decisions to be taken. For example, it was to Mrksic that Dr. Vesna Bosanac, the director of the hospital, turned on 19 November when it came time to arrange the evacuation. That's at trial judgement 137. It was with Mrksic that the ECMM monitors met on 19 November also to discuss the evacuation. That's at trial judgement 139. It was with Mrksic that a UN diplomatic and fact-finding mission met on 19 November so that it could gather information about whether UN peacekeeping forces should be sent there. Even men of the same rank acknowledged that it was Mrksic who was the area commander; for example, when the three JNA counter-intelligence officers that you've heard about today, Colonels Vujic, Tomic, and Kijanovic, arrived from Belgrade in November, they reported to Mrksic, the Chamber find; they don't order him. That's at 169 of the judgement. Once these colonels arrive at Velepromet on 19 November, they asked Mrksic for reinforcements. They don't order him to provide them. That's at 173 of the judgement. And, finally, when these colonels have seen enough at Velepromet, and the Chamber finds that they saw there men who had been beaten and the colonels themselves were threatened by the TOs who had gathered there, they tell Mrksic they won't take any further part. That's at 172 of the judgement. One of them, Colonel Vujic, tells Mrksic the situation is, quote, "an attack against you as a commander." And that's at 174 of the judgement. This, Your Honours, is an explicit recognition that it was Mrksic who was in charge and that he was failing in his duty to protect the prisoners. Coming just a day before the events of the 20th, his words proved prophetic. Now, the evidence also showed that Mrksic was directly and personally involved in every aspect of the prisoners' evacuation, transportation, and security on the last day of their lives, and if I could direct Your Honours' attention to the screens, that would display a Powerpoint presentation. And as you can see, Your Honours, at 6.00 a.m., Mrksic orders the evacuation of the prisoners from the hospital. The night before, of course, he had appointed his subordinate, Veselin Sljivancanin, to evacuate the prisoners and to be responsible for their transport and security. That's at 295 and 400 of the judgement. At around 10.30, Mrksic sends his Chief of Staff, Miodrag Panic, to a meeting of the SAO government. He tells Panic to instruct those present that he would accept and act in accordance with the decision of the government meeting as to what should be done with the prisoners. After the evacuation from the hospital, Mrksic orders the prisoners to be held at the JNA barracks in Vukovar, countermanding his earlier order that they be sent to Sremska Mitrovica. At 11.00 a.m., after the buses had arrived at the barracks, Mrksic bolsters their security after hearing an alarming phone call from Susic, a military police commander, and I'll explain a little bit about that in a minute. Finally, at around 2.00 p.m., Mrksic orders the prisoners to be taken to Ovcara Farm. Then, as I'll explain, Mrksic makes the final order of the day to withdraw the military police from the 80th -- of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Now, this evidence shows and the Chamber found that Mrksic was receiving constant updates from his subordinates, who were telling him that the prisoners were being abused. At 10.30 a.m., he hears from his Chief of Staff, Panic, from the JNA barracks, and, again, I'm not sure if Your Honours' attention is directed to the screen, but there is another presentation. At 11.00 a.m., he hears from one of his military police battalion commanders, Susic, also reporting from the barracks. Sometime after 3.00 p.m., Mrksic hears again from his Chief of Staff, this time about Ovcara. Sometime in the afternoon of the 20th, he hears from Vukasinovic of his security organ, also reporting about Ovcara. He hears twice, once during the briefing and once shortly after, from Vojnovic, the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, also reporting about Ovcara. Finally, after the briefing, Mrksic hears from Vukosavljevic. This is Vojnovic's security chief from the 80th Brigade, also reporting from Ovcara, and what he heard from these men was indeed alarming. From Susic, he hears the safety and security of these people at the JNA barracks are in danger. From Vukasinovic, reporting about Ovcara: "I propose that we strengthen security detail there because I have a feeling there might be some problems in the future ." From Vojnovic, whom he hears from twice, Vojnovic testified and the Chamber found that he told Mrksic: "At Ovcara, there's a mess. I saw a man hit one of the prisoners with a rifle-butt as he was passing through the gauntlet up to the entrance of the hangar." From Vukosavljevic, he hears, also reporting from Ovcara: "A group of men at Ovcara were threatening the prisoners being secured by the 80th Motorised Brigade, and the group of men contended that the prisoners belonged to them and not to the 80th Motorised Brigade." The Chamber finds then that throughout this day, Mrksic was involved in every major decision regarding the transport and security of these prisoners and that he was given constant updates from his subordinates about their safety. It is, therefore, illogical to believe that Mrksic would not also have made the final decision of that day, to leave the prisoners in the hands of the TO and the paramilitaries. The only reasonable explanation is that the withdrawal order came from the same man who gave each of the other important orders that day, Mile Mrksic. But the Chamber did not rely, as the Defence indicates today, solely on Mrksic's position of authority to conclude that he was the one who issued the order. It also delved into the evidence of the transmission of the order itself and came to the only reasonable conclusion that it was Mrksic who issued that order. Specifically, the Chamber found a line between Mrksic and the withdrawal -- and again, I'm illustrating my point on a slide here, Your Honours. First, Mrksic ordered Borce Karanfilov, one of Sljivancanin's security officers, to withdraw the 80th Motorised Military Police Company from Ovcara. That's at 293 and 329 of the Trial Chamber judgement. Karanfilov, in the Chamber's finding, conveyed this order to Captain Dragan Vezmarovic, who was the commander of the 80th Motorised Military Police Company. That's at 277 and 321 of the Trial Chamber judgement. Now, Vezmarovic says that this occurred about one and a half hours after he arrived at Ovcara, which in his testimony was about 5.00 p.m. After Karanfilov arrived at Ovcara, the Chamber found, he and Vezmarovic, the commander of the Military Police Company who was then providing security, had an extensive conversation. Karanfilov told Vezmarovic that the, quote: "Vukovar TO was to take control of the security of the building" - that is the hangar - "and the prisoners." Per arrangements made at a meeting. That's at 277 of the Trial Chamber judgement. Karanfilov then introduced the TO commanders to Vezmarovic and told the military police commander that they would be the ones who would take charge of the prisoners. Vezmarovic asked the commanders whether they had enough men to perform all the security tasks. He was told that they did, and he withdrew his policemen by 9.00 p.m. at the latest. That's at 277 of the Trial Chamber judgement. Other evidence corroborates both the timing and source of this order, the Chamber found. The Chamber found that Milorad Vojnovic, commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, reported to Mrksic about what he saw at Ovcara, again, twice that evening, first at the evening briefing - that's at 315 of the judgement - and again shortly after it ended, and that's at 316 of the judgement. During this second conversation, Mrksic asked Vojnovic something along the lines of, What were you doing there? That's at 281 of the judgement. This shows, in the Chamber's finding, that Mrksic was surprised to discover that the military police were still at Ovcara, and this, the Chamber finds, is because Mrksic had already ordered the military police to withdraw from that place. Vojnovic then turned to Drago Vukosavljevic, his security chief, telling him to go to Ovcara and order the military police to leave. That's at 281 of the judgement. Vukosavljevic arrived at Ovcara at about 8 p.m., but he found that Vezmarovic, the military police commander, and his policemen had already left the hangar and were preparing to leave the area, and that's at 276. Now, this confirms, Your Honour, that the military police had already received their marching orders from Mrksic via Karanfilov. The evidence fits together. Now, as Defence has pointed out, the evidence as to this order was not without its contradictions. Karanfilov told the Chamber that he had never had a conversation with Vezmarovic on the 20th of November, 1991. The Chamber was thus faced with a conflicting account. Resolving this inconsistency ultimately boiled down to one essential question: Was the Chamber to believe Karanfilov and throw out the testimony of Vezmarovic, Vukosavljevic, and Vojnovic, or was the Chamber to believe the latter three and reject the testimony of Karanfilov? In evaluating, as it must, the credibility of each of these men, the Chamber found that Karanfilov was not reliable and that the others were. The Chamber was entitled to make these findings, and indeed, they were reasonable ones. As to Karanfilov, the Chamber found he was personally biased - this is at 282 of the judgement - and that his testimony contained inconsistencies which could not be rectified with other evidence, like whether and where he spoke with Sljivancanin on 20 November, and I refer you to 282 of the judgement for that. The Chamber also found Karanfilov not credible as to other material aspects of his testimony, and rather than going into those, I'll refer Your Honours to paragraphs 216 and 300 of the judgement. On the other hand, the Chamber found that the testimony of the other three men to be credible, and Vezmarovic in particular had no personal interest in contriving a story, the Chamber found. If he had, he probably would have come up with a better story, in the Chamber's finding. If I could draw your attention to the screen again. Now, remember, Your Honours, that Karanfilov was the subordinate of Veselin Sljivancanin. He worked for the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade. Now, as Defence has pointed out, Vezmarovic was a member of an entirely different unit, the 80th Motorised Brigade. Vezmarovic normally reported to Vojnovic, the commander of that brigade. The men had the same rank, that of captain, and in the Chamber's finding, if Vezmarovic was in the business of making up stories, why would he invent a story that contained such an unusual chain of command? Receiving an order through his ordinary chain of command, the Chamber found, would have been more likely to be believed and, if you're in the business of making up stories, would also have the added benefit of alleviating Vezmarovic for being on the hook for leaving Ovcara without the proper order or approval of his commander, and the Chamber made this analysis at 283 of the judgement. Another piece of evidence has been raised in today's hearings, Your Honour; that is, that of the war diary of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Defence says that indicates the military police did not leave until 2235, rather than sometime before 9.00 p.m., as the Chamber found. Well, this argument ignores the fact that the Chamber considered this evidence, and that's at 286 of the judgement, weighed it against all the other evidence, and found that the entries could not be relied upon. The Chamber considered this and made its determination based on the totality of the evidence, as the Chamber must. The Chamber also considers other possibilities in its arrival at the conclusion that it was Mrksic who had issued that order. It asks: Could Vezmarovic have been acting on his own? That is, Vezmarovic, the commander of the Military Police Company. Could Vojnovic have been acting on his own? Did Sljivancanin have a role in the transmission of this order? The Chamber considered each of these questions and came to the only conclusion reasonable from the evidence, that the order can only have originated from Mrksic, and that's at 321. You've heard a little bit about that line today as well. Defence, at page 9, line 11 of today's hearing, seems to imply that this conclusion, which is an indication of the circumstantial aspects of certain parts of this evidence, cannot constitute proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and this conclusion is obviously incorrect. As to these particular witnesses, the Chamber rejects, based on its evaluations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wood. I just wanted to make sure that at one point or another, you or your colleagues from the Prosecution will address the questions which we listed on the Prosecution -- the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, I'm best placed to answer that question. The Prosecution will address all of the four questions that Your Honours have posed, two of which relate directly to the Prosecution's appeal and will be dealt with on Friday, and two of which -- actually, excuse me, three of which are directed to the Prosecution's appeal and will be dealt with on Friday, and one of which will be dealt with this afternoon in relation to Sljivancanin's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Brady. I just wanted to make sure that this is on your schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Now, again, getting back to the consideration of the credibility of Vojnovic and Vezmarovic, I'll just refer Your Honours to paragraphs 279 and 321 of the judgement for that. Essentially, the important point is the Chamber made these assessments after seeing these men testify and weighing their evidence against all the other evidence and found that they were reliable, and of course, these are reasonable conclusions. As to Sljivancanin, the Chamber rejects the idea that this order could have been transmitted through him, and I will refer Your Honours to paragraph 661 of the Trial Chamber judgement, where the Chamber finds he didn't arrive back until after 8.00 p.m., that is, back at Negoslavci, whereas the Chamber found that Karanfilov, who is the agent for transmission -- transmitting the order, could have been around Negoslavci at the time the order was given. And in answer to the Defence contention that it's illogical that an order would have come from Mrksic to Karanfilov, the Chamber also finds that it was not unusual for Mrksic to deal directly with his security organs that day. It finds, for example, that he dealt with Vukasinovic directly. That's at 285 of the judgement. Against all of this, the Chamber considered the unique role that Mrksic played with respect to the prisoners on this last day of their lives. Mrksic, the Chamber finds, was directly concerned in dealings that day between the JNA and the SAO government. This is at 285 of the judgement. The Chamber found virtually, inevitably, Mrksic had a direct responsibility in the making of decisions and their implementation in the course of that process; again, at 285. Based on a totality of the evidence, after hearing all of the testimony, weighing that against all the other evidence, the Chamber concludes the order could only have come from Mrksic. This was the only reasonable conclusion available from the evidence. Mrksic clearly disagrees with this finding, and he makes his opinion plain in submissions today. He fails, however, to show how this essential finding, that is, that he was the one who gave that order, was one that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have made. As the Prosecution has pointed out in its response brief, Mrksic's attacks on appeal and what you've heard today are either re-arguments of his case at trial or subject to summary dismissal, per Brdjanin and other appeals case. Each fails its essential burden to show that the Chamber's findings were those that no reasonable Chamber could have made. The Chamber was entitled to make this conclusion, Your Honours. More importantly, the Chamber was right to make this conclusion. Mrksic's arguments should be dismissed. And I'll turn the floor over now to my colleague, Ms. Lewis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Lewis, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEWIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will be addressing Grounds 1, 2 and 8 of Mrksic's appeal, in which he argues that the Trial Chamber erred in convicting him for the crimes committed at Ovcara because responsibility in fact lay with the security organs and the local command. I will firstly address Ground 2, in which he argues that it was the security organs who were responsible for the evacuation because this function was within their remit and chain of command. Consequently, he argues, they were responsible for the crimes. I will then address Grounds 1 and 8, in which he argues that it was the local command who were responsible. To turn, then, to Ground 2, Your Honours, this argument fails for two reasons. It fails firstly because, as my co-counsel Mr. Wood has argued, the Trial Chamber found that the evacuation of the prisoners was ultimately within Mrksic's command and control and that he made each of the critical decisions which led to the order to withdraw and the crimes against the prisoners. In view of the fact that Mr. Wood has dealt with this fully, I won't address it further. I will, however, address the second basis on which this argument fails, which is that it fundamentally misunderstands the counter-intelligence function of the security organs; in particular, that in relation to the evacuation, the security organs would have had primary responsibility for the counter-intelligence component of this operation, the triage of the prisoners, and that for this component they would have been responsible to their superior security organs, but that for the other component of the evacuation, the operational components, the actual securing and transport of the prisoners, they would have been subject to Mrksic's command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEWIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Trial Chamber found that for counter-intelligence functions, the security organ was responsible to their superior security organs, but that for all other functions, they were subject to the unit commander. In relation to OG South, the Trial Chamber found, therefore, that the subordinate security organs would have reported to Sljivancanin and that he would have had the ability to direct, coordinate, and guide their work, but that he could not command them; trial judgement paragraphs 127 and 398. For this conclusion, the Trial Chamber relied on a number of pieces of evidence. Firstly, it relied on Exhibit 107, the Rules of Service of the security organs, in particular, paragraphs 16 and 18. Paragraph 16 provides that the security organ is directly subordinated to the commanding officer of the unit, in this case, Mrksic. Paragraph 18 provides that the security organs of the superior command provide assistance to those organs and organise, direct, coordinate, and supervise their work; trial judgement paragraph 128. The Trial Chamber also relied on the testimony of Theunens, the Prosecution's military expert, who testified that in an establishment unit, security organs exist only with respect to counter-intelligence activities, and the reference is 10867 to 868, and trial judgement paragraph 129. Your Honours, Theunens testified further that the relationship between the security organs of a higher and a lower command was not one of command and control in the military sense but, rather, one of specialised guidance. Whilst the security organs reported to the security chain and received guidance, they were subordinated to the unit commander; 10725 and 10858. This testimony was confirmed by the testimony of Sljivancanin himself, who described the relationships between security organs of a higher and lower level as a management relationship and not one of command. Sljivancanin testified that there was no dual chain of command, that security organs, like any other officer, were subordinated to their unit commander, but that in relation to their counter-intelligence functions, because of the confidential nature of these functions, they received guidance and advice from within the structure of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEWIS
utterances.text: I apologise. And the reference is 13440 to 41 and 13434 to 36, and trial judgement paragraph 127. Your Honours, these -- this finding was confirmed by the testimony of other witnesses to whom the Trial Chamber also referred: the testimony of Colonel A gotic in the Slobodan Milosevic trial, which was admitted in this case as Exhibit 75 at page 23271; the testimony of Vojnovic, the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade at 8827; Vukosavljevic, the security chief of the 80th at 8651 to 8652; and Karan, a security officer subordinated to Sljivancanin at 15539 to 40, and again, the reference to the judgement is paragraph 127. So, Your Honours, if we consider the evacuation operation against the background of the reporting and command structure of the security organs, it becomes clear, one, Mrksic's argument fails; the evacuation operation had two components. We know that it had a counter-intelligence component, the triage, identifying which of the prisoners had been members of the armed forces and had committed crimes during the hostilities. This function fell -- was the primary responsibility of the security organs, and we see that from the testimony of Major Pringle, an expert military witness for the Prosecution at 11101 and again from the testimony of Captain Karan at 15555. Major Pringle testified that in view of the essential nature of this component of the evacuation, it was not surprising and one would have expected that the security officers would have been present at the various locations throughout the day. Your Honours, it is for this reason that the Appeals Chamber should reject my learned colleague from the Defence Mr. Vasic's suggestions that there was something sinister in this. To the contrary, it was fully consistent with the Trial Chamber's findings regarding the role of the security organs on that particular day. So, Your Honours, for the other components of the evacuation operation, the operational components, the actual securing and the transport of the prisoners, the security organs would have been subject to the command of Mrksic. Your Honours, I'm not going to deal in detail with the arguments that Mrksic raises in his brief. Our response to this is fully canvassed in our response brief. I will, however, touch on two of the specific arguments that he made today. In his submissions, Mr. Vasic argued that the testimony of Vujic and Sljivancanin show that the security organs were acting under the command of the Security Administration. To the contrary, Your Honour, the testimony of these witnesses merely confirm the Trial Chamber's findings; that whilst they would have been receiving direction from the superior security organs for the counter-intelligence aspect of the evacuation, the triage, for all -- in all aspects, they acted subject to Mrksic's command, and the relevant references are 4626 to 27 and 4521 to 22, that's for Vujic, the testimony of Sljivancanin to which I have already referred, as well as the following references: 13991 to 92 and 13617. Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber should therefore reject Mrksic's submissions with regards to the security organs, and I will now proceed to address his arguments regarding the role of the local command. Mrksic has argued that as the local command, it was Vojnovic who was responsible for the crimes at Ovcara, either because he failed to adequately secure the prisoners, or because he permitted the withdrawal, or, alternatively, for having himself issued the order to withdraw. This argument should be rejected because it ignores critical findings of the Trial Chamber. In particular, Your Honours, it ignores the fact that Mrksic was ultimately found responsible for his own positive conducts. He was found responsible for having issued the order for the 80th Motorised Brigade to withdraw. That's trial judgement paragraphs 321 and 329. Furthermore, Your Honours, this argument ignores the fact that the Trial Chamber found that at the relevant time on the 20th and 21st of November, Vojnovic and the 80th were subject to Mrksic's command. Therefore, as my co-counsel Mr. Rogers has argued, even if they were in their own duties, they were at all times under Mrksic's command, and the ultimate responsibility vested with him; trial judgement paragraphs 69 to 73, and 111 to 113. Under Ground 8(a) of his submissions, Mrksic argues that after he departed to Belgrade, he was no longer in command and that responsibility again vested with Vojnovic. Once again, Your Honours, this argument fails because it ignores the Trial Chamber's findings that Mrksic was held responsible for his own conduct for withdrawing the 80th Motorised Brigade, and that at the relevant time the local command was subordinated to OG South and ultimately to Mrksic, and again, the references are paragraphs 69 to 73 and 321 to 329. To conclude, Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber should reject Mrksic's arguments that it was Sljivancanin and the security organs and Vojnovic and the local command, in effect, everyone and anyone but him, who were responsible for the crimes at Ovcara. This ignores the Trial Chamber's findings. It ignores the fact that Mrksic, a commander of, if not the, then a premier unit of the JNA, had been specifically tasked with carrying out the evacuation, that Mrksic had issued each of the critical decisions which culminated in the crimes against the prisoners. Mrksic ordered Sljivancanin to carry out the evacuation. It was Mrksic who ordered Panic to attend the meeting of the SAO government and communicate that he would act upon their wishes. It was Mrksic who ordered the prisoners to be held at the barracks to await this decision, and it was Mrksic who ordered the prisoners to be transferred to Vukovar. In addition, it was to Mrksic that everyone turned with their concerns about the threat that was presented by the TO to the security of the prisoners. His Chief of Staff, Panic; the commander of one of his military police battalions, Susic; Vojnovic; and Vukosavljevic, the commander and the security chief of the 80th; and the security officers from Belgrade, Vujic, Tomic and Kijanovic, all brought their concerns to Mrksic, and despite these repeated warnings, despite being told over and over and over about the threat presented by the TOs and the paramilitaries, Mrksic did not act to increase the security and remove this threat. Instead, he withdrew the only protection that the prisoners had, which culminated in their cruel treatment, torture, and ultimately their murder. Your Honours, we request the Appeals Chamber to reject Mrksic's appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, could you tell us, when did Sljivancanin learn of Mrksic's order to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEWIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Trial Chamber found that Mrksic communicated the order to Sljivancanin, the oral order, on the afternoon of the 19th, the day before -- I'm sorry, Your Honours, I may have misunderstood the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEWIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I apologise. I misunderstood the question. The general answer is that it was around 8.00 p.m. on the 20th, but this will form a part of Ms. Brady's submissions, and she will deal with it in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So Ms. Brady will return to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will be spending a fair amount of time on this question on Friday, in which I will set out the evidence and the findings that we rely on to show that the only reasonable conclusion that must be drawn from the totality of the evidence is that when Mr. Sljivancanin returned to Negoslavci at about 8.00 p.m., he must have learnt then that Mrksic had ordered the withdrawal of the JNA -- the remaining JNA units at Ovcara. But I think it might be better to hear my submissions, which are fairly lengthy on this point, on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEWIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if there are no further questions, that concludes our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Since there is only ten minutes to the time we have fixed for the ending of this morning's session, I will not ask at this stage the appellant to reply, but we will have our break now and resume at 1400 hours sharp, 2.00 sharp. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. We are now about to start the second half of the proceedings today, and before we do so, I would like to inform my colleagues and the parties of a slight change in the schedule for the presentation of their arguments because we are informed by the Court officers that we are all able to sit in court for one hour and forty-five minutes at a time; otherwise, we risk running out of tape and the proceedings won't be audio-recorded. I have slightly adjusted the schedule for this afternoon. My colleagues will find in front of them the corrected schedule, and I would ask the Registrar kindly to circulate this amended timetable to the parties. We will start from reply by the appellant Mrksic, who will have 30 minutes to complete his case of the appeal for Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My learned friends from the Prosecution in response to our appeal tried to plead in relation to the orders that were issued by Colonel Mrksic as commander of Operations Group South and to base on that their assertion that, therefore, he must have issued the order on the withdrawal of the military police. On the one hand, this has to do with orders that he had to make as commander, which is only natural, and the withdrawal of the police is something that he's being charged for in terms of individual responsibility, and there is not a shred of evidence to that effect in the case file. You will not find a single witness having stated that Mile Mrksic said that he had issued an order to withdraw the forces from Ovcara. Even Vojnovic doesn't say that. He says unequivocally that he had not said that to him; rather, that that is how he understood his question, What are you doing there? However, this is happening precisely because in the judgement, material evidence is being superseded, material evidence such as diaries and orders. It is superseded by formal statements of witnesses, and therefore, the Trial Chamber has a problem in terms of resolving timing issues. They conclude that what is written in material evidence is not correct and that what witnesses like Panic and Vojnovic state is correct. The former remembered only in 2001 that the evacuation of the hospital happened on the 20th of November, rather than the 21st, and the latter only after 1998 remembered that on the 20th of November, he did see Mile Mrksic after all. I have to remind my learned friends and the Appeals Chamber of the fact that the prisoners of war went to Sremska Mitrovica on the basis of a regular procedure. You will see that from the judgement where the Trial Chamber asserts that on the 18th of November, a group from Mitnica went to Sremska Mitrovica. When the group went to Sremska Mitrovica, when they arrived in Ovcara, they spent the entire night there, and lists were made and a triage was carried out, but Mile Mrksic had nothing to do with that whatsoever. I believe that that is not even being challenged. That is to say, going to Mitnica via Ovcara is something that was established by the organs who dealt with this matter. My learned friends say that the 80th Brigade did not have orders to prepare for guarding prisoners of war at Ovcara on the 20th of November. I believe that that is not the case and that we should look at Exhibit 375, the entry of 1800 hours on the 19th of November; also, Exhibit 891 that my learned friends invoked in the sense that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 819.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This does not infringe upon the position of the POWs. I don't believe that that was dealt with properly because what is stated here is that they were interrogating potential crime suspects, war crime suspects, and then they decided whether they would hand them over to other organs without consulting the command and the commander. THE COURT REPORTER: I'm sorry, Your Honour. There seems to be a problem with the LiveNote feed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The problem is with what? THE COURT REPORTER: With the LiveNote feed. It has stopped and we have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Can we start now even if you fill in later the -- it's working now? It's working now, right? Okay. We will now resume, and if you have to fill in later a few missing words, you'll do that. Okay, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to continue from where the transcript stopped. So my learned friends say that the Command of the 80th Brigade had not been informed that on the 20th of November, POWs from the hospital would be transferred to Ovcara. I believe that that is not right. Therefore, we should see 375, Exhibit 375, the entry for 1800 hours on the 19th of November. As for Exhibit 819, I believe that it clearly demonstrates that the security organs are in charge of triage and uncovering perpetrators of war crimes and crimes in general. In practice, after interrogating these persons, they decided on their further processing or handing them over to other organs without consulting the Command or the commander of the unit about that. I have already referred to Exhibit 419 and the order of Mile Mrksic for the evacuation of civilians and the sick and wounded from the hospital, and the fact that when an order is issued concerning an assignment, it is not issued in two parts as is determined by the Trial Chamber but in a single part, and that is precisely what we have in writing in the case file. The decision on the establishment of a town command on Ovcara was not made by Mile Mrksic because of the transfer of prisoners of war but, rather, on the basis of an order issued by the Command of the 1st Military District and the Supreme Command. I've already spoken about that; namely, this was meant to ensure the safety of civilians and their property in areas where there were no functioning civilian authorities. Also, I have to say that my learned friends tried to tell us that Colonel Mrksic was actually a person who was asked about everything. As a commander, he was supposed to be asked about most things. However, the evidence does not show this, and this is what we say in our response to the appeal, and that is that he received the representatives of the EC Monitoring Mission because Witness Kipper shows that it was only for a few minutes that he received even Cyrus Vance. It was a question of protocol, just receiving him for a courtesy call for a few moments, and that basically it was Colonel Pavkovic and the officers from the 1st Military District that were in charge of this. As for Vujic, Tomic, and Kijanovic, it was not established in the evidence that they asked Mrksic for some kind of reinforcement with regard to Velepromet. I think that the fact that Witness Jaksic came to Mrksic at the request of the minister of justice does not lead us to infer that Mrksic was a person who was asked about POWs. That is what my learned friends are trying to suggest. Rather, it was a consequence of the fact that the government of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, on the 20th of November, 1991, came to Vukovar for the first time ever since the war conflicts had broken out and that they were not aware of the situation on the ground at all, and they did not know who was in charge of what. Further on, the essence of the problem was, when we look at the trial judgement, is the timing, the time-frame that the Trial Chamber tried to fit into the witness statements of those witnesses who they trusted. If this was not confirmed by material evidence and the statements of other witnesses or with the fact that Mile Mrksic between 7.00 and 8.00 p.m. on the 20th of November went to Belgrade, they needed to deal with the time-frame in the following way: They moved the government session to an earlier point in time, although we have 268-269, that's the exhibit number of the video footage showing that the session could not have started before 2.00 p.m., and the judgement says that it started between 10.00 and 11.00 a.m. Also, the buses could not have been in the yard of the barracks while the session was still on because they were already in Ovcara by 1.30, and the session started only at 2.00 p.m. Then, also, there is a move in terms of time when the briefing started. Trifunovic claims that it started at 5.00 p.m., and he's the chief operations officer of the Command, and that time is moved to 1800 hours, whereas 1800 hours is actually the time when reports are sent to the higher command. This is done in order to move time ahead and to establish that Mile Mrksic could have issued an order to have the military police withdrawn before he went to Belgrade. Finally, perhaps a crucial matter in this entire judgement is the withdrawal of the military police, which according to the operations diary of the 80th Brigade took place at 2235 hours; that is to say that this particular point in time was confirmed by the Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and he is in charge of the accuracy of the documents of the unit. If this is correct, and it is correct, then the Trial Chamber made the wrong conclusion when they concluded that the withdrawal took place by 2100 hours. Then that would have been reflected in terms of the fact that that kind of order for withdrawal could have come only half an hour earlier, and by then Mile Mrksic had been in Belgrade for quite a while. Therefore, he could not have issued this kind of order. This also has to do with the assertion made by my learned colleagues in relation to Captain Karanfilov. We heard their explanation today in terms of who's telling the truth, he or the witnesses from the 80th Brigade. However, even today, I did not hear and I did not find in the judgement any proof indicating that Karanfilov was in Negoslavci at the time when the Trial Chamber found that allegedly Mile Mrksic issued an order on the withdrawal of the military police. The Trial Chamber does not give an explanation to that effect, and it does not explain how this kind of conclusion is supported. Therefore, I believe that this conclusion cannot be beyond a reasonable doubt, and I don't think that any reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Captain Karanfilov received the order precisely in Negoslavci, and precisely from Mile Mrksic, and precisely at the Command of Operations Group South. Quite simply, there is not a shred of evidence attesting to that. This conclusion is actually amplified by what my learned friends said in their response to the appeal. If you recall, they said that this order, as established by the Trial Chamber in the judgement, is an unusual chain of command rather than the regular chain of command and that something that happened there was a situation that was out of the ordinary. In order for a reasonable trier of fact to make a conclusion beyond any reasonable doubt, there would have to be proof justifying this unusual conclusion, that is to say, one that deviates from the rule, from everyday practice. We have an unusual situation here, and there is not a shred of evidence to the effect that this had actually happened. That is the main problem with regard to this judgement. So it would have been normal for orders to be issued down the chain of command, or if it involves security organs, to go down the security line. Here, the Trial Chamber finds that the commander, through the security officer, issued an order. There is no evidence to prove that, and, on the other hand, there are no evident reasons why such a thing might occur. My learned friends also stated that within the scope of his activities, the security organs also engaged in counter-intelligence work, the detection of crimes and criminals, but not the transport and security of prisoners of war. I must draw the Appeal Chamber's decision to paragraphs 124 and 127 of the appeal, where a part of a telephone conversation is paraphrased. This conversation took place between Mr. Sljivancanin and Tumanov -- or, rather, General Vasiljevic, and here Tumanov says: [In English] "You know routine, send them to Sremska Mitrovica for interrogation, and that was the end of the conversation." [Interpretation] Commenting on the conversation with General Vasiljevic: [In English] "We briefly discussed the telegram, as well, that I received from him. I said that without any interview, We shall send also suspects to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica, and that there were organs there that would further investigate these persons." [Interpretation] So the movement of these persons is clearly agreed upon along the security line. Another attempt by my learned friends was evident today to present Mile Mrksic as the only person who might issue such an order, thus supporting the decision reached by the Trial Chamber, and that attempt consisted in their saying that the unit he commanded was a unit established as such units should be established and not a chaotic unit. Orders are not issued to well-organised units in unusual ways as seems to have been the case here. We cannot consider a unit to be orderly when we wish to consider it to be orderly and to be disorderly when it serves our purpose to be viewed as chaotic. As regards the situation, I think it is clear to everyone here that there were many representatives of the highest military organs present at Ovcara, both security and others, and I really think that the conclusion we presented in our oral arguments, that it would have been impossible for Mile Mrksic to issue an order which would then remain a secret to all for such a long time, especially as we heard before the Chamber that the security organs on that same night -- the night sent to [indiscernible] Colonel Petkovic and Babic and later to General Aleksandar Vasiljevic information about this. So it is impossible to believe the conclusion of the Trial Chamber that the brigade commander could ensure such secrecy concerning the event which followed. To this day, we do not know when this order was issued because it's neither in the judgement, nor have my learned friends been able to tell us this today. The Chamber left open two options before or after the briefing because it also left open Mrksic's departure for Belgrade. However, my colleague explained today why it was impossible for such an order to be issued either before or after the briefing. If it has been established beyond reasonable doubt and if it is the result of testimonies of officers of the 80th Brigade, why, then, did Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic come to Operations Group South if his units had been ordered to withdraw from Ovcara? And this is stated by Witness Trifunovic, a Prosecution witness. So to conclude, I believe that there is not a shred of evidence to show that Mile Mrksic issued the order on the withdrawal of the military police of the 80th Brigade from the Ovcara Farm either to Captain Karanfilov or to Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, and I therefore submit that his guilt in -- that his culpability has not been established beyond reasonable doubt. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you for completing your presentation on time. We appreciate that, and we will now move on to the appeal of Mr. Sljivancanin. Will that be Mr. Lukic, Mr. Bourgon? Mr. Lukic. I apologise. My distinguished colleague Judge Guney has a question. You will have to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Counsel, you alleged that the Chamber concluded that the order for withdrawal just before -- or just after the regular daily briefing in Ovcara, so Mrksic's argument failed to show why no reasonable trier of fact could have reached this same conclusion. Could you develop on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: In addition, of course, Vukasinovic twice informed Mrksic about the events of Ovcara, and the other inform of Vukasinovic at Ovcara on 20 November 1991. So if you can develop on that as a whole. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber established the alternative, that Mile Mrksic issued the order on the withdrawal of the military police either before or after the regular briefing. Before the regular briefing, he would have issued this order to Captain Karanfilov, but he could not have done so before the regular briefing because at the briefing itself, had such an order been issued, it would have been mentioned. Mile Mrksic would have reported this. He would have said that his unit was supposed to withdraw from Ovcara, and there would have been no logic in him doing it through the security officer when he would have the commander of the unit with him at the meeting and he could have issued the order in the regular way. None of the numerous witnesses who attended that briefing said that that was the topic or a topic discussed at the briefing. Furthermore, none of the witnesses say that Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic informed Colonel Mrksic about the critical situation at Ovcara. Witnesses Trifunovic, Gluscevic, Panic, say nothing about what Vojnovic said to Mrksic at that meeting. Vojnovic himself up to 1998 never said he said anything to Mrksic concerning the events at Ovcara. After the briefing, it would not have been possible for this order to be issued because Witnesses Gluscevic, Sljivancanin, and Coric concluded a series of meetings that Mrksic had in the Command before leaving for Belgrade, driven by Colonel Coric, in front of the -- who was waiting for him in front of the building, so he had no opportunity to issue the order to Captain Karanfilov. He had no time to see Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, either, after the briefing because -- and the Defence submits that they did not meet as Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic himself said up to 1998. After the conversation with Vukosavljevic, as we heard today from my colleague, he heard that Vukosavljevic had allegedly been at Negoslavci, and as he believed Vukosavljevic, he accepted this story that they had been there together. This story, in fact, in the view of the Defence is evidence which cannot be accepted beyond reasonable doubt and which is contradictory to other evidence which the Trial Chamber accepted in the alternative. They accepted that Mrksic may have left Belgrade between 1900 and 2000 hours. As regards the activity concerning the security at Ovcara, that was the command of the -- the town command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and they were supposed to provide security, and Mrksic resubordinated more than a thousand soldiers to that unit. But from the operations log of the Motorised Brigade, Exhibit 371, we see that there is an order on reinforcing that unit, and between 1700 and 1800 hours Mrksic called the office of the motorised APCs, and he ordered that this unit be given to Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic and to be at his disposal if needed. I don't know if I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to use the break to introduce another member, and we have Marie Claude Fournier joining us for this second part of the hearing. Before I begin, I just want to say that it is our idea for me to talk about the introductory part, and I'm also going to discuss the first ground of the indictment, and then Mr. Bourgon is going to provide his arguments for the other counts of the indictment and also respond to certain questions that you have put and to tell you that the response to issue number 3 that you put earlier to the Prosecutor, we will also be leaving for Friday because it's logical then that that be part of the themes that we will be discussing on Friday. Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin at the very beginning would like to emphasise its position. The Trial Chamber judgement, in relation to the findings on the basis of which his criminal responsibility was established, is based on important errors which have brought us to a miscarriage of justice. In our appeal, we would like to show that the only possible decision which can come out of that is an exonerating sentence, or an acquittal, or a retrial. We would like to point out the most significant positions to indicate, also, the way of the -- the best and the easiest way to understand the position of the Defence, and we would like to leave no matters that are unclear or any dilemmas after our discussion. The Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin, from the beginning of the trial, was not a passive part and did not wait for the Prosecution on whom lies the burden of evidence, and we did not wait for them to present their case and make all the assertions. The Defence understood this trial as the way to reach the full truth of Ovcara -- about Ovcara and not a trial about the counts in the indictment. By carefully analysing the judgement, we have established that the Trial Chamber established key facts on events at Ovcara on the basis of the presentation of evidence of the Defence of Veselin Sljivancanin, and in many parts of its judgement it affirmed the positions of his defence. Can you please see how much the Prosecutor refers to today to the testimony of Witness Panic, even though the Prosecution and Mr. Mrksic's Defence did not actually call him as a witness, even though he was on their list, and who happened to testify on behalf of Sljivancanin. From the beginning of the trial, we emphasised that we believed that the key moment of that entire tragic 20th of November, 1991, was the government meeting of the SAO Krajina, and after that the change of the evacuation plan of the prisoners of war instead of taking them to the prison in Mitrovica, to take them to Ovcara, and this is the point from which everything else proceeded in the wrong direction or it all went downhill. Another key event, according to the judgement, is the decision to withdraw the security detail from Ovcara. This decision had as its direct consequence the unimpeded access to the prisoners by members of the TO and the paramilitaries, which, as the Court established, led to their killing. The participation of Sljivancanin in these events did not exist in any form. His defence in relation to these facts was consistent and clear. Your Honours, Sljivancanin decided to sit in the witness chair right at the beginning of his defence, and he was directly cross-examined for 16 hours both by the OTP and by Mr. Mrksic's Defence team. In many parts of his testimony, the Trial Chamber relied on his testimony and based its findings on that testimony. However, some parts of his testimony and his defence were not accepted by the Trial Chamber. This refers to the assignment and the role he had in the hospital evacuation operation, but as it will turn out in the end in the judgement, also on the fact which became key in terms of his responsibility and his testimony that he was not at Ovcara at any point on that day, the 20th of November, 1991. Your Honours, Veselin Sljivancanin was not at Ovcara or in the barracks on the 20th of November, 1991. We assert this, and we did so from the very first beginning of the presentation of our case. This was stated in our pre-trial brief, in our opening statement, and that was also our theory or thesis throughout the whole presentation of evidence during trial. When you carefully review our appeals from the first ground of our appeal, it will not be necessary, Your Honours, to analyse more, either Sljivancanin's appeal or the position of the Prosecution in terms or in respect of his responsibility. The Sljivancanin Defence is aware of the practice of Appeals Chambers, which is very restrictive in re-evaluating the established factual matters from the actual trial, giving precedence to the Trial Chamber in its assessment of evidence. But when these conclusions do not satisfy the standard "beyond any reasonable doubt," then they inevitably lead to a miscarriage of justice. So in its written arguments, and we are going to present a part of that orally today, the Defence showed that the Trial Chamber committed errors when it concluded that Sljivancanin was at Ovcara on the 20th of November, that he could have seen the beatings of the prisoners, and that he was aware of prior criminal conduct by members of the TO, and that it was his duty to prevent further assaults or attacks on the prisoners. After these errors in their factual conclusions, the Trial Chamber reached erroneous legal findings that by his omission to act, he significantly contributed to further crimes of torture in the afternoon of the 20th of November, 1991. All the facts on the basis of which the Trial Chamber established the responsibility of Mr. Sljivancanin can only all together lead to the conclusion of his responsibility as established by the Trial Chamber. If the Appeals Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber erred in any factual conclusion on which it relies on for Sljivancanin's conviction, that inevitably must lead to acquittal. In case the Appeals Chamber establishes that the appellant was not aware of charges for aiding and abetting by his omission to act and that such a form of criminal liability does exist and which we assert that the Prosecutor articulated only in his final brief, only a new trial with a very precise indictment could be in the interests of justice. And, finally, at the end of this introduction, just a few more words about the assertions from Mr. Mrksic's appeal. The Sljivancanin Defence spent a long time considering whether it should address the Appeals Chamber with a request that it was responding to this appeal. The thesis of Mr. Mrksic's Defence to a considerable degree is based on the responsibility of Mr. Sljivancanin, and we did provide arguments in our final brief about that particular theory of Mrksic's defence because that was the first time we encountered it in their final brief. This theory that is articulated in their final brief and is being repeated throughout their appeals brief is based on their own evaluation of evidence and by referring to some theories which were not articulated in the course of the trial itself and were not substantiated by evidence. The Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber reaches decisions on the basis of their own assessment and not on the basis of somebody else's interpretation of the evidence. This is our only comment. Now I'm going to move to arguments that relate to Ground 1 of our appeal. The presence of Sljivancanin at Ovcara, as this was established in the judgement, has become a fundamental question of fact in terms of establishing his responsibility. In the event that the Trial Chamber did not conclude that he was in front of the hangar at that time, it would not have established the existence of his criminal responsibility. The Trial Chamber exclusively on the basis of the testimony of one witness, P-009, established that Sljivancanin was at Ovcara on the 20th of November, 1991. When a certain fact which in many aspects is crucial for the establishment of possible responsibility of the accused can be established by the Trial Chamber from the testimony of only one witness, the Court must approach that task with particular caution, especially if that evidence contradicts a large number of other evidence on the same fact. The Trial Chamber in the judgement referred to some standards for which it said that it applied in the assessment of those key facts, and these are paragraphs 11 to 16 of the judgement. The essence is that in view of the contradictory facts, motives, and a large passage of time from those events, the Trial Chamber approached its evaluation of evidence with particular care. The strategy of the Defence in disputing this assertion from the indictment was clear: to ask each, I underscore, each and every witness who testified that he was at Ovcara at the same time and at the same place as asserted by P-009 was to ask whether he saw Sljivancanin there. According to the understanding of the Defence, if this simple analysis is applied to such an important question in the judgement, the question which presents the crux of possible criminal responsibility, precise arguments must be provided. No reasonable trier of fact can be left in a dilemma about the possibility of the existence of a different conclusion. The Trial Chamber as cited in the appeals brief in reference to this conclusion, the presence of Sljivancanin at Ovcara, committed important errors. Among them, they are: One, did not compare the testimony of Witness P-009 with testimony of other witnesses who testified contrary on this particular matter, that they did not see Sljivancanin at Ovcara. In reference to the group of witnesses who were prisoners from the bus, the Trial Chamber in paragraph 382 refers to only two who did not see Sljivancanin. Besides these two, at the trial P-031, P-011, Cakalic, Karlovic, and Dodaj said the identical things during the trial. Dodaj, P-011 -- yes, I mentioned that, and Dodaj. And we are going to provide some explanations in reference to Dodaj. Two, the Trial Chamber erred by mentioning in the judgement erroneous conclusions about the reasons why they did not accept evidence from other witnesses who claimed the opposite and which the Trial Chamber analysed. We referred to this in our appeal in paragraphs 155 to 169. Three, erroneously evaluating evidence that relates to the circumstances in which Witness P-009 allegedly previously saw Sljivancanin, which constituted the basis of recognising him in the first place. We refer to this in paragraphs 83 to 117 of our appeal brief. Further, by stating contradictory conclusions, the Trial Chamber erred because in reference to the key fact, Sljivancanin's presence at Ovcara, after evaluating the evidence, it relied on two witnesses who actually speak completely opposite things about that fact, and we refer to this in our paragraphs 63 to 81, and then also erred by not considering the inconsistencies in the testimony of P-009 with other conclusions of the Trial Chamber and his motives to conceal the facts, and these are our paragraphs 131 and 145. And the Trial Chamber also did not pay attention to their own relevant conclusions about the presence of Sljivancanin in that period in the hospital, and these are paragraphs 147 to 145 of our appeal. This erroneous approach and erroneous evaluation of the evidence led to conclusions that no reasonable trier of facts would reach, especially not as the only possible conclusion. Some of these errors we are going to dwell on in more detail now. By relying on the evidence of Witness P-009, the Court established that P-009 saw Sljivancanin at Ovcara at around 1430 or 1500 hours on the 20th of November. Witness P-009, in the findings of the Trial Chamber previously, stood in front of the hangar, observed the beating, and then went behind the hangar, returned some 15 to 20 minutes later, and then saw Sljivancanin passed by him and entered the hangar. According to him, at that point in time the prisoners were already inside the hangar. This is paragraph 377 of the judgement. The location and the timing that the Court concluded, on the basis of this testimony, are quite precise. In its further analysis of the reliability of the testimony of this witness, the Trial Chamber had a clear and responsible task: to compare that evidence with other evidence, primarily with statements of other witnesses who asserted that they did not see Sljivancanin there. Probably, any witness, including P-009, is something about which the Trial Chamber had to ask itself the following question: Was the witness in a position to observe the area in front of him? Was he convincing? Did he have any reason to be insincere, and what can be reliably established on the basis of the testimony of each particular witness? A considerable number of witnesses on which the Court relied about facts surrounding the hangar at the time that P-009 refers to was so convincing for the Trial Chamber that on the basis of their testimony, they established facts. They were, thus, credible. Besides describing what they saw happen, in which the Court relied on their testimony and the Court trusted them, they also said that they did not see Sljivancanin at that time. The Trial Chamber also reaches a contradictory conclusion in its conclusion in paragraph 382, when it says that Witnesses Berghofer and P-030 in view of the circumstances were unable to observe all the officers in front of the hangar, and thus, they reach a conclusion which is contradictory to their other conclusions. The Court trusted these same witnesses in its conclusions when it -- when they described who participated in the beatings; paragraphs 938, 939, 932, and 931. The Prosecution's assertion in its response --

utterances.text: My distinguished colleague Judge Guney has a question.

You argue that only the willful failure to discharge a duty which imply the culpable intent of the accused can lead to the individual criminal responsibility. utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The assertion by the Prosecution in its response that the prisoners in the bus were afraid and thus focusing on their survival cannot be the basis for accepting their testimonies when other relevant facts are established based on the testimonies of these same persons who described in details officers, their ranks, and their uniforms. When Sljivancanin's Defence got the reply from all the people who were on the bus that they did not see Sljivancanin at Ovcara, the Prosecution did not ask any of them in redirect about what is now being asserted in the appeal. They want to avoid it being stressed that these witnesses were in such a situation that they were unable to observe everything that was in front of the hangar. Did these witnesses have any reason to conceal Sljivancanin's presence at the hangar? No. They testified in great detail to Sljivancanin's appearance and his physical description when he was in front of the hospital, and they did not conceal their animosity and their hostility towards him. The Trial Chamber did not obtain an answer from the witnesses to the effect that they were unable to observe the area in front of them, so all this is based on supposition, not on evidence, and this constitutes an error. Another group of witnesses who did not see Sljivancanin in front of the hangar at that time are three JNA officers: two Prosecution witnesses, P-014 and Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, and also Lieutenant-Colonel Panic. The Trial Chamber gave its reasons why it's possible that these witnesses did not see him. These are paragraphs 378, 381, and 380. But the Trial Chamber made an error here when explaining why the testimonies of Colonel Panic and P-014 do not cast doubt on the testimony of Witness P-009. The reasons for their rejecting their testimony about this fact contradict other conclusions reached by the Trial Chamber on the presence of these witnesses at Ovcara at the same time. In another paragraph of the judgement, paragraph 309, the Trial Chamber states that Vojnovic and Panic were talking in front of the hangar and that they were seen doing so by P-014; paragraph 254. If the Court relied on Witness P-014 and believed that he was there while the beatings before the hangar were going on and he left while the beatings were still going on, it could have reached only the following conclusion, that Colonel Panic arrived while the process of bringing the prisoners into the hangar was still ongoing, and then the other conclusion cannot be sustained, the one from paragraph 380, that Panic didn't see Sljivancanin because he arrived later on. On the other hand, if the Trial Chamber established that P-014 saw Panic and then believed Panic that he arrived when the process of taking the prisoners into the hangar was already finished, as they did in paragraph 258, then Witness P-014 was at Ovcara even after the prisoners were taken into the hangar. Then the reason from paragraph 381 as to why the Court did not give credence to Witness P-014 cannot be sustained, and we gave a detailed explanation of this in paragraph 36 of our response. I do understand that this is rather complex. The issue of the credibility of these witnesses has to be evaluated. Vojnovic and P-014 and Witness Panic, the first two being Prosecution witnesses, did they have any reasons to be partial? Certainly not. None of them could have a motive for concealing the fact if Sljivancanin had really been there. In fact, they would have welcomed that. If possible, they, in a situation where they were discussing the security of prisoners of war in the area, would it have been possible for them not to notice a person such as Sljivancanin? No reasonable trier of fact could reach the conclusion reached by the Trial Chamber. And, finally, an error which completely brings into question the conclusion regarding the reliability of the testimony of Witness P-9 is the testimony of Witness Dodaj Hajdar, the evaluation of that testimony and the failure to compare that testimony with the claims of P-009. Witness Dodaj, a Prosecution witness, a prisoner from the bus, according to paragraph 236 of the judgement, left the bus before last, did not go into the hangar, and stood there in front of the hangar with another three prisoners who had been separated off and several JNA officers. The Court mentions two lieutenant-colonels and one captain. In paragraph 70 to 74 and paragraph 129 of the appeal, we provide detailed references to his testimony, which we feel are very important and to which the Trial Chamber also refers. Dodaj states that he, as he stated in his testimony, stood there observing the beatings and the other events and the people in front of the hangar for one or two hours, and he responded when asked directly that he did not see Sljivancanin at Ovcara. Before that, he observed him for more than half an hour from very close by in the hospital, and in relation to his testimony about that fact, that he did not see Sljivancanin at Ovcara, the Trial Chamber gives credence to that testimony saying that it is persuasive in paragraph 386. So, Your Honours, we have two testimonies about the same fact occurring at the same time in the same place. One witness claims to have seen Sljivancanin at Ovcara - that's P-009 - and the Court gives him credence in that, and the other one who says he did not see Sljivancanin - Witness Dodaj - but the Court believes this witness also. The Prosecution is trying to mitigate this error made by the Trial Chamber by arguing that Dodaj was afraid and was thus unable to observe properly the area in front of him. However, the Court has established that this witness was convincing and that he did not see Sljivancanin. The Prosecution could have asked Dodaj whether he was in such a state that he was unable to fully observe the area in front of him, but the Prosecutor did not ask him that question, him or any other witness, for that matter. In spite of his fear, the Court believed Dodaj and considered his testimony to be persuasive. The Prosecutor has no arguments to argue that this is an error made by the Trial Chamber, and then the Trial Chamber erred in not comparing two persuasive testimonies which it had before it. When it had before it two such testimonies, both of them persuasive, the Trial Chamber should not have left this hanging in the air. The Trial Chamber did not explain on what it based its conviction that Witness P-009 was persuasive, in spite of the fact that it's so contradictory to the other findings of the Trial Chamber. Witness P-009 claims that he passed by Sljivancanin and entered the hangar and that there were no other people there, either soldiers or officers, in the area in front of the hangar. Contrary to this, the Trial Chamber established that when the prisoners were leaving the bus and immediately after they entered the hangar, both Vojnovic and Panic and two lieutenant-colonels who questioned Dodaj and his group were there; Vojnovic and Panic, according to paragraph 258, and the two lieutenant-colonels in paragraph 236. P-009 completely contradicts the finding of the Chamber that he did not see the beatings in the hangar when he went in. He entered the hangar almost immediately after the POWs were brought in, and after a certain time he took out Witness P-030 and 6287. But the Court, in spite of the testimony of Witness P-030, made its finding about the beating in the hangar in paragraph 237, and I refer you to paragraphs 952, 953, 954, and 956 of the judgement. These all refer to the testimony concerning the beatings by Witness P-009, who was in the hangar at the same time. This shows beyond any doubt that P-009 was not telling the truth in his testimony because he was trying to mitigate his own participation in the events. Could we please move into private session so I can make a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness, who was at Ovcara as a member of the TO and before that in the barracks at Velepromet on the 19th of November and everywhere, he was seen with weapons, recognised by witnesses, did he have an answer to be partial? The witness should have been [as interpreted] asked whether he saw Sljivancanin on that day.
