But regardless of the fact that all these witnesses are Prosecution witnesses, they had a hostile attitude towards Sljivancanin considering him to be the person who separated them off at the hospital, they were all very precise in their statements. A correction to the transcript, pages -- page 25, they were asked: The witnesses were asked whether they had seen Sljivancanin on that day. In paragraph 369, the Trial Chamber analyses the testimonies of only three of these witnesses. Apart from these three witnesses, all the other witnesses from the bus, another six witnesses, said they hadn't seen Sljivancanin at the barracks, but the Trial Chamber does not mention them. These were all Prosecution witnesses, and we refer to them in paragraphs 98 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 99, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and 88 of our appeal brief. The Trial Chamber found that these witnesses were unable to describe in detail all the events in front of the bus because of the conditions in which they found themselves, but this again contradicts the finding where such witnesses were given credence when establishing the events concerning the bus; paragraphs 216 to 217 of the ... At the barracks, just like at Ovcara, only P-009 did not see what the Trial Chamber established from the testimony of all other witnesses, a key event, and that was when the prisoners were being transferred to the sixth bus. That was the only time when there was physical contact and abuse of the prisoners, and this is on transcript page 6279. The Prosecutor makes their analysis of evidence by asserting that it's possible that P-009 arrived after these persons were moved to the sixth bus and before the bus left in the direction of the hospital, but there is a trap there because this collides with the conclusions of the Trial Chamber, which found that 30 minutes after the arrival of the bus, the TO members were taken away from the barracks, were removed from the barracks. So how can P-009 then testify about so many events at the barracks if he was only there for a few minutes? This is impossible. He had to have been there much earlier, and then he could not have failed to see when more than ten prisoners were beaten in the way that the Court established in paragraph 217. Thus, the Court believed the witness which was the only one to see Sljivancanin of all the witnesses who were there, when none of them saw them, and who was the only one who did not see the beating at the barracks and at the hangar at Ovcara, which was something that all the others did happen to see. Is that a witness on whose testimony exclusively the Trial Chamber based its conclusion about the responsibility of Sljivancanin? If the key conclusion of the Trial Chamber in the judgement of Sljivancanin is based on the testimony of only one witness, then the Trial Chamber must prove the reliability and credibility of that testimony. These two categories cannot be accepted a priori as arising from what the Trial Chamber only said, that they believed somebody and they did not believe someone else. If the conviction of the Trial Chamber about the credibility and reliability of the testimony cannot be checked and evaluated as being the only possible conclusion, then that brings into question the need for an appeals proceedings in general. Your Honours, we expect that you will, in the role of a reasonable trier of facts, will in detail and comprehensively evaluate the credibility and reliability of this testimony and evaluate the errors committed by the Trial Chamber in establishing key facts on the basis of his statement. And, finally, the Trial Chamber makes one more mistake in which the conclusion about Sljivancanin's presence in the barracks cannot be believed as credible. If Sljivancanin was seen in that area of the barracks and spent there all the time, as described by P-009, before the sixth bus left for the hospital - paragraph 371 - how is it possible that Sljivancanin waits for that bus at the hospital as was the testimony of witnesses from that bus - this is T-660, and these are Witnesses P-012, 487, Witness Wilhelm, and transcript 2826, Bucko - and question them? Which reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Sljivancanin could have been at Ovcara in front of the hangar at 14, 13, or 1500 hours if in the judgement the Trial Chamber previously establishes that Sljivancanin was at the hospital at the time of the departure of the convoy with the civilians at 1400 or 1430 hours; paragraph 376. Even though the Prosecutor responds to the Prosecution -- to the appeal, suggests that this was a small distance that Sljivancanin could have covered within that time-frame, the Trial Chamber established differently. According to the Trial Chamber, the buses needed half an hour to go from the barracks to Ovcara. These are paragraphs 222 and paragraph 234. From the hospital where Sljivancanin happened to be between 1400 and 1430 hours, as established by the Trial Chamber, this could have been a much longer road, and we would like to ask you to look at Exhibit 156. This was a map. And I would like to conclude with the following: Your Honours, the Trial Chamber in its evaluation of evidence, in reference to the presence of Sljivancanin at Ovcara, committed a number of errors which led to the conclusion that no reasonable trier of facts could reach, thus resulting in a miscarriage of justice for which reasons we believe that the judgement cannot stand. Thank you very much. If there are no questions, my colleague will cover our other grounds of appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Stephane Bourgon, and I will continue the presentation of our arguments this afternoon on appeal from the judgement that was rendered in this case. It is my understanding that my colleague used up 44 minutes of our time and that accordingly I have 46 minutes left. I will try to speak for 30 and then take the break, and according with the new schedule issued by the Presiding Judge at the beginning. Mr. President, I will begin by saying a few words concerning our submissions on omission liability, which is Ground 2 in the appellant's brief. I will also answer question 4, which is found in the addendum to the scheduling order for this appeal, and then I will move on to Grounds 3, 4 and 5. Regarding omission liability, it is our submission as argued in our brief that this specific form of omission liability as identified by the Trial Chamber in the judgement does not exist. That is not to say, Mr. President, even if we take into consideration the fact that before the International Criminal Court the situation appears to be entirely different, we are not saying that an accused cannot be found guilty for an omission pursuant to the Statute of this Tribunal. Nonetheless, it is important to note that the International Criminal Court paints an entirely different position with respect to omission, and that tells us that this is a very special and exceptional form of criminal liability and that it is of the utmost importance when dealing with omission liability to precisely identify the parameters of this type of liability before it can be applied to any situation. In the Prosecutor versus Tadic, the Appeals Chamber has recognised that a person may be found guilty for a culpable omission in the presence of a positive duty to act if there was a deliberate failure to fulfill this duty. This refers, Mr. President, to omission as a principal perpetrator and not as an accomplice, and it requires the proof that the accused shared the mens rea of the perpetrators. In other words, it must be shown that the accused intended the consequences of the crime being perpetrated or that he must have been aware of the consequences and consented that they would occur. Although the Trial Chamber in this case did refer in its reasoning to the fact that Sljivancanin had a duty to act, it did not find him guilty for a culpable omission as a principal perpetrator. Another type of omission liability found or recognised in the Statute of this Tribunal can be found, as we know, in Article 7(3), which deals with the responsibility of commanders and other superiors. Pursuant to this article, a commander can be found criminally responsible for a violation committed by a subordinate over whom he exercises effective control if he has reason to know or if he knows that this subordinate is about to commit a crime or is committing a crime and he fails to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent him from doing so. When I talk about identifying the parameters of omission liability, this is what I am referring to. In the light of general principles of criminal law, this type of omission liability, Mr. President, the command responsibility, is exceptional. Normally, a person can only be found guilty of a crime by being involved in some way in the commission of that crime and, of course, by having the necessary intent. If we look at Article 7(3) of the Statute, the commander is not involved in the commission of the crime, and it need not be shown that he shared the mens rea of the perpetrator. Nonetheless, because responsible command is one of the foundations of international humanitarian law and because if there is one person who can prevent a crime committed by a subordinate, it is his commander, for this reason, this exceptional type of liability is accepted and recognised. That being said, Mr. President, command responsibility is framed very precisely with a view to avoiding any type of strict liability. Firstly, it would have to be shown that there was a superior-to-subordinate relationship which existed between the commander and the perpetrator. Secondly, the commander, knowing that the subordinate is about to commit a crime or is committing a crime, will only be found guilty if he fails to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent his subordinate from committing this crime. The words "reasonable" and "necessary" are important here, and that is with a view to avoiding what I mentioned earlier, strict liability. It must be noted, finally, with respect to Article 7(3), that the responsibility of the commander pursuant to this article focuses on preventing a subordinate from committing a crime and not on preventing a crime from being committed. It is our submission, Mr. President, that these are the only two types of omission liability which are recognised pursuant to the Statute of this Tribunal: a culpable omission as a principal perpetrator or command responsibility pursuant to Article 7(3). There is, of course, another type of responsibility, which although it looks like omission liability, in fact, it is not, and this is what has been referred to by the approving spectator or the bystander. Indeed, if a person is present at the scene of the crime, and the mere presence of that person provides encouragement or moral support to the perpetrators of the crime, then it is accepted and it is recognised that this person may be found guilty as an accomplice if the person knows that his presence is indeed assisting the commission of the offence by legitimising in the eyes of the perpetrator, which is very important, the commission of the crime. This is not, Mr. President, in our submission, omission liability because the presence of the accused in such a scenario at the scene of the crime assisted the perpetrators. It had an effect on the illegal acts of the perpetrators and contributed to the commission of the crime. A question was put to my colleague earlier concerning commission by omission. This is exactly what we refer to. It looks like omission liability, but it is not. It is commission by omission. In our written pleadings, we referred to one author, but there are many others, Michael Dutweiler. He explained the difference between omission proper and commission by omission. For commission by omission, it is necessary for the person to have a material ability to do something, but by failing to do what the person has the material ability to do, he actually participates in the crime. Encouragement, providing encouragement is exactly commission by omission. For us, to have commission by omission, it has even to go further than the normal criteria for aiding and abetting, although there are different positions, we recognise, in the case law of this Tribunal and that of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. Mr. President, in this case the question is the duty of the person. Is it relevant that the approving spectator had or did not have a duty to prevent? What we are saying, Mr. President, that in such a case it is not necessary for the approving spectator to have a duty to prevent the subordinate from committing a crime or to commit [sic] anybody from committing that crime. That is not to say that the duty will not become a relevant consideration. The duty may be a relevant consideration if the perpetrator, for example, is aware that the person would normally stop him from committing the crime. Then it may be a relevant consideration because in the eyes of the perpetrator, he will say, This person has a duty to stop me, I know the person has a duty to stop me, and the person is not stopping me; therefore, I can continue in full impunity. However, the duty is not a prerequisite. The difficulty in this case, Mr. President, is that the Trial Chamber used a mix of culpable omission liability, of aiding and abetting, as well as some notions of command responsibility. Indeed, the Trial Chamber found that the accused had a duty to act, that he was present on the scene, that he saw a crime and did not take action, that the crime was not committed by his subordinates, and that the perpetrators did not see him and did not know him and were not encouraged in any way by his presence. In our submission, on the basis of these facts, the Trial Chamber could not have found the accused guilty of any type of omission liability, whether it be called culpable omission or aiding and abetting by omission, and there was no -- any type of encouragement provided to the perpetrators. Does the Trial Chamber find the accused guilty pursuant to a form of omission liability which, in our submission, does not exist? In fact, it amounts to strict liability. Indeed, if the presence of Sljivancanin did not provide encouragement or moral support, the fact that he had a duty to protect the prisoners of war at Ovcara, if he did, and that having seen the beatings, he did not take action, is not sufficient for him to incur criminal liability, unless, of course, the culpable omission be proven. In this regard, the nature of the duty to protect prisoners of war, which is not a duty which implies that prisoners will automatically be safe if the duty is not fulfilled or is fulfilled, the nature of that duty must be considered. The extent to which the duty was or was not fulfilled must also be considered. In other words, if we accept that type of omission liability, what about if the duty was partly fulfilled? How do we analyse? We cannot under the model or under the mode of liability identified by the Trial Chamber. It cannot be, Mr. President, that a person having a duty to protect, who fails to act pursuant to this duty, in all or in part, will be automatically -- or will automatically incur criminal responsibility. There's another reason why this type of omission liability does not exist. In fact, it would render Article 7(3) of the Statute obsolete. In all cases where the commander had a duty to protect prisoners of war, there would be no requirement to use Article 7(3), and therefore, the Prosecutor will be dispensed from proving the superior-to-subordinate relationship. If we accept what the Trial Chamber used as a mode of liability - that means that for aiding and abetting, the person has a duty to protect, the perpetrators were not the subordinate of the accused, the person did not provide moral encouragement to the perpetrators, but the person nonetheless failed to take action - we cannot do away with Article 7(3) of the Statute, considering its importance for international humanitarian law. I now come to question 4 in the addendum to the scheduling order. In this question, the Appeals Chamber requests the Defence to clarify the following: If the Appeals Chamber recognises aiding and abetting by omission in the specific form which was used by the Trial Chamber in this case, and if the Appeals Chamber concludes it is a valid mode of liability, then what is the extent to which - and the question is quite precise - if at all the concrete influence and the decisive effect criteria, which we advance in our written pleadings, are relevant to the assessment of an actus reus of aiding and abetting by omission? First, Mr. President, it should be mentioned that both criteria, the decisive effect criteria and the elevate degree of concrete influence criteria, were mentioned by -- the first one by the Trial Chamber in the Blaskic case, and then it was mentioned again by the Appeals Chamber, and the second one, the elevated degree of concrete influence, by the Appeals Chamber in the Oric case. In both instances, the Appeals Chamber was discussing omission liability but did not pronounce and did not identify the essential elements thereof, and the Appeals Chamber was quite clear, leaving open the possibility that actus reus of aiding and abetting could be fulfilled by an omission. That's the first consideration. Secondly, in our view, Mr. President, the Appeals Chamber -- if the Appeals Chamber does recognise aiding and abetting by omission in the specific form identified by the Trial Chamber in the judgement, then the crux of the matter becomes the following question: Everything will lie in the meaning to be given to rendering practical assistance, which has a substantial effect on the perpetration of a crime, which as we know is the applicable criteria for actus reus for aiding and abetting in the case law of this Tribunal. In this regard, it is our submission that the criteria, decisive effect and the elevated degree of concrete influence, which of course we took from decisions rendered by the Appeals Chamber, they are relevant in that they are illustrations of the fact that the omission must have assisted the perpetrators, it must have had an effect on the illegal acts of the perpetrators, and it must have contributed substantially to the commission of the crime. We could describe omission liability or this link, this relationship between the omission and the perpetrators in many ways. What we do know is that a cause-to-effect relationship is not required and that the omission cannot be a precondition or, to use the words of the Appeals Chamber, a condition precedent to the commission of the crime as set out in -- it was in the Blaskic Appeals Chamber judgement. What is important is that the assessment, whether the omission had a substantial effect on the commission of the crime, it must be conducted from -- by looking at the crime which was committed and not at the omission itself. In other words, from the point of view of the perpetrators, did the omission of the accused assist them or have an effect on their illegal acts or contribute substantially to their committing the crime? Another way to look at this is that if the omission did not change or alter the conduct of the perpetrators, then it cannot be said to have had a decisive effect on the commission of the crime or a concrete influence on the perpetrators. This, of course, requires a careful fact-based inquiry because there may well be external factors to the omission itself which will help in determining whether such omission had or did not have a substantial effect on the commission of a crime. As argued in our submissions related to Ground 5, which I will come to in a minute, it is our submission that in this case, even if the Appeals Chamber recognises aiding and abetting by omission as identified by the Trial Chamber in this case, that even though Sljivancanin would have been present and would have taken no action, this had no effect whatsoever on the perpetrators in this case. I now move to Ground number 3, which as you know, Mr. President, concerns the alleged error committed by the Trial Chamber in finding that Sljivancanin had a legal duty to protect the prisoners of war held at Ovcara. It is our respectful submission in this regard that on 20 November 1991, Sljivancanin did not at any time have a legal duty to protect the prisoners of war held at Ovcara. This ground of appeal, which includes five sub-grounds and which is directly related to part of the Prosecution's second ground of appeal, which will be argued on Friday, we rely almost entirely on our written pleadings, which are quite lengthy and detailed. Accordingly, my submissions today will be limited to a few specific issues. It is our submission that the duty to care for prisoners of war, the origin of the duty comes from the Geneva Conventions, more specifically, Geneva Convention 3, Articles 12 and 13. This responsibility is imposed on states on the high-contracting parties. The states have this responsibility, and the duty is triggered when they have prisoners of war in their custody. States delegate this responsibility to their agents. When a military unit holds prisoners of war in its custody, the de jure agent of the state is the commander, in this case, the OG South commander or the 80th Motorised Brigade commander when the prisoners were in Ovcara. Now, to fulfill this duty or responsibility, the commander uses the resources at his disposal, including his officers, but the commander cannot absolve himself of this responsibility or does not delegate this legal duty by issuing tasks and orders. Accordingly, whatever order or task was given to Major Sljivancanin did not impose on him a duty or responsibility which may give rise to his criminal responsibility any more than any of the officers of Operational Group South involved in the events related to the prisoners of war as a result of the measures taken by Commander Mrksic for this purpose. Should the Appeals Chamber conclude otherwise and hold that there was a specific duty imposed on Sljivancanin on 20 November in relation to the prisoners of war at Ovcara, because this is where the crimes were committed, then it is our submission that this duty was at an end immediately after the meeting of the SAO government where the plan was changed entirely. Whereas the prisoners of war were supposed to go to Sremska Mitrovica, the plan was changed, and Sljivancanin was kept out of the loop. Sljivancanin was not involved in the transmission and the implementation of the order to send the prisoners of war from the JNA barracks to Ovcara. Had the Trial Chamber found that he was, we believe that this finding cannot stand. Firstly, the Trial Chamber found no direct evidence of the involvement of Sljivancanin in the giving or implementation of this order. Secondly, the Trial Chamber's conclusion in this regard - that was at paragraph 659 of the judgement - rests on eight other findings which it made, such as the presence of Sljivancanin at the barracks on the morning of 20 November, and all of these findings, in our submission, constitute either unreasonable inferences or were adopted on the basis of circumstantial evidence having little or no probative value. In these circumstances, it is our submission that the Trial Chamber's findings related to the involvement of Sljivancanin in the transmitting and the implementation of the order to send the prisoners to Ovcara cannot stand. Significantly, if Sljivancanin was not involved in the implementation of this order, any duty he might have had at the time to protect the prisoners of war was at an end. Some of the findings that we have to look at in this regard include the fact that when Sljivancanin directed the triage at the hospital, he did not know that prisoners of war would be taken to Ovcara; judgement 657. He did not know, either, about the meeting of the SAO government, which is something he learned much later. The decision to keep the buses at the JNA barracks waiting for the outcome of the meeting of the SAO government was taken by Mrksic; judgement 300. The decision to send MPs from the 80th Motorised Brigade at Ovcara to be ready to secure the prisoners was also given by Mrksic through his command staff with no involvement from Sljivancanin; judgement 305. Veselin Sljivancanin, as demonstrated by my colleague, was not present at the JNA barracks in the morning. Veselin Sljivancanin was not present at Ovcara on 20 November. In these circumstances, it is our submission that after the meeting of the SAO government, it terminated, at the latest, Sljivancanin was excluded from the task related to the prisoners of war. Veselin Sljivancanin completed his task related to the evacuation of the civilians at the hospital, and we know from there where he was on the basis of his testimony. We know that Sljivancanin was not involved in any way with the withdrawal order. The Trial Chamber judgement found that. I have one more sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me. You are slightly over time, and we have to stop now for 15 minutes, and then you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will stop. I had one more sentence before breaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay, let's have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Simply to say that he did not have any duty bestowed on him by Mrksic who handling and directing this undertaking of OG South related to the prisoners of war addressed and was addressed by other officers than Sljivancanin from that point on. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We will now have a 15-minute break and then we will resume [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Bourgon, I must tell you today I am troubled by your vision of -- very formalistic vision of the 3rd Geneva Convention. I'm afraid that if your suggestions were taken seriously, duties of states would be greatly diluted. You know the famous statement in the Nuremberg trials that states acts through individuals, and if Sljivancanin was given certain responsibilities for the evacuation and for caring for POWs, wouldn't his duties continue under the 3rd Geneva Convention until he could hand those duties over to someone else who could assume responsibility for the POWs? Can you abandon POWs at one point in time to a programme awaiting for them outside? What happens when there is no formal delegation at all of power on the part of the state, but there are POWs -- soldiers who surrender to another unit? Under certain notions of the 3rd Geneva Convention, that unit has to assume welfare and the responsibility for those agents. I must say that I am very troubled by those implications, what you are telling us about this possibility of bing, bang, ending responsibility, just leaving them out to be murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe I can clarify -- I appreciate your question, Mr. President, and maybe I can clarify my position. Prisoners of war cannot be abandoned at any time, so if this is what comes out of what I said, then I apologise because this is not what I meant at all. What I meant, Mr. President, is that the duty to protect prisoners of war, it belongs to the person in whose custody prisoners of war are, and with respect to the matters and to the facts of this case, the prisoners of war were in the custody of Operational Group South, and the commander of Operational Group South is Mile Mrksic. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Was Sljivancanin given by Mrksic certain responsibilities or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then, Mr. President, what we say is that if he was given -- we say -- we, of course, in our brief, we argue that he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Now assume for a moment that he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We argue, but assuming that he was given, then argument, Mr. President, if he was given some taskings to accomplish, he can be, of course, found to have failed in his duty to accomplish a task given to him by his commander. But unless you will find this duty was a culpable intent with respect to the prisoners of war, he cannot be found guilty of a crime. That's what we are saying. On the other hand, Mr. President, the commander who had those prisoners in his custody because they were in the custody of the unit, then it's a different matter because the duty belongs to him at the time, the de jure responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But the most immediate and direct responsibility pertained to Sljivancanin as the head of the military police unit, who was given -- assuming he was given responsibilities by Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you for this observation. It is very important because one way which an officer within the military unit which has the custody of the prisoners of war could, by his attributions, be responsible for the prisoners. He could have responsibility for the prisoners, but we heard the Prosecution this morning say that the security officer did not have this responsibility for prisoners of war, and Sljivancanin was not the head of the military police; far from it. All the evidence on the record clearly showed that he was not -- he did not -- he did not exercise command over the military police. If one person exercised command over the military police, it was Mile Mrksic, and not Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm sure we will hear comments from the Prosecution on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I go on -- I'm moving on, Mr. President, Your Honours, to I Ground 4 dealing with our submissions that there was no omission on the part of Sljivancanin, simply because if he was in Ovcara, contrary to our arguments, then he did not see the beatings and the crimes being committed there, and if he did not see those crimes, then there cannot be any omission on his behalf. Mr. President, on the basis of the lack of evidence on the record as to what Sljivancanin did or did not do at Ovcara, this, in our view, is the reasonable conclusion. Of course, Mr. President, we maintain that Sljivancanin was never at Ovcara on 20 November 1991, and we insist on this. As demonstrated by my colleague, there's just too many hoops which the Trial Chamber went through to arrive at this conclusion. So now I find myself arguing in the abstract, what if he was there? Does that make him guilty of a crime? Firstly, our submission in this regard should not be considered in any way as recognising that Sljivancanin was there. Moreover, it is critical in our assessment that the responsibility of Sljivancanin must be assessed precisely on the basis of the evidence on the record. Why is this important? Because the Trial Chamber found Sljivancanin guilty because he had seen and not taken action. That's basically the reason why he was found guilty by the Trial Chamber. Now, of course, in order to trigger his duty to protect, in the sense of triggering an omission, he must have seen the beatings taking place, and he must have been aware, and he must have failed to take action. The Trial Chamber in this case did not find that Sljivancanin saw the mistreatment. The Trial Chamber said he must have seen the mistreatment, which is quite different. In order for the Trial Chamber to conclude that he must have seen the mistreatment, it must be the only reasonable conclusion based on the totality of the evidence. As demonstrated in our written pleadings, this is not the case. The Trial Chamber firstly found that he did not enter the hangar, which means that the only mistreatment he could have seen is that which took place outside when the prisoners were taken out of the buses, went through the gauntlet, and entered the hangar. This is very important because my colleague demonstrated that the only witness who saw Sljivancanin there, who would have seen Sljivancanin there, he said that when he saw Sljivancanin, the buses were gone and everybody is in the hangar. So what could Sljivancanin see? He did not see the beatings, Mr. President. He could not see the beatings -- the prisoners going through the gauntlet. Now, there are two findings of the Trial Chamber in this regard, at paragraph 380 and 663, and then those two findings are contradictory to its own finding regarding what it accepted from Witness P-009. The question becomes, Mr. President: How long was Sljivancanin at Ovcara, if he was there? The problem is we have no evidence. When did he arrive? We don't know. When he left, we don't know. What he did see, we don't know. What he did, we don't know. How did he travel to Ovcara? We don't know. Was he accompanied by anyone? Did he have a driver? Did he speak to anyone? We know absolutely nothing concerning the involvement of Sljivancanin at Ovcara. That's the crux of the matter, Mr. President. For each of these questions, not one iota of evidence, and the Prosecution can point to now. Now, we compare that to the testimony of Sljivancanin, who made it clear that he was not there. It follows in these circumstances that the -- by inference, we cannot say that Sljivancanin was there for 1, 2, 5, or 15 minutes, so we must rely on what's there, and what's there is that when P-009 would have seen him, the buses are gone, and everybody is in the hangar, and he did not look into the hangar. That's what we have to rely on in part of the evidence, so thus, no reasonable trier of fact could conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that he must have seen the mistreatment of the prisoners. One last argument is very important in this regard because it also goes with our first ground of appeal, is that if we accept that he was in Ovcara and that he did not do anything, it leads to a completely absurd result. This means that he would have travelled to Ovcara immediately one minute after finishing up his duty with the civilians in the proper way. He arrives at Ovcara; nobody sees him. Upon arriving at Ovcara, he sees the prisoners of war being mistreated; he sees the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade; he sees the Chief of Staff, two senior officers to him; he doesn't go into the hangar to see what's there; he doesn't interact with anybody in Ovcara; he leaves the area with no one seeing him; having left the area, doesn't say a word to anybody the whole day. Basically, he ran away, completely disregarded the duty which might have been given to him or bestowed on him by his commander. At night, he meets Vukasinovic, and he would pretend that he wasn't aware of Ovcara. He meets his commander. He would have avoided to speak of Ovcara. This leads to an entirely absurd result, accepting the fact that either he was in Ovcara, which was our Ground 1, or that he must have seen the beatings. I move to Ground number 5, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You have five minutes, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thought I had ten, Mr. President, based on my estimate, but if I -- I will accelerate. I only have Ground 5 left, which is -- I will address only two sub-grounds and not the third one, the first one being that, in our submission, he did not have the necessary substantial contribution, if you accept aiding and abetting, simply because his acts had no effect whatsoever on the actions of the perpetrators, and that's very important. Why this act? Because the Trial Chamber found that there was no encouragement or moral support and because when we look at the situation and the totality of the evidence, what is in the mind and what is -- what are the perpetrators doing, the fact that Sljivancanin shows up there has no input whatsoever or no implication or effect on their actions. The argument to the contrary, saying that because he did not take action, they acted with impunity, is misconceived. That's not the way to assess aiding and abetting. The way to assess this argument is by looking at the effect on the perpetrators. The perpetrators saw those senior officers present. The perpetrators saw those people in the JNA taking action trying to stop them. The perpetrators did also -- were the same people who were at the JNA barracks the previous morning when the JNA took action to stop them, so they know that if they are going to be stopped, the people who can stop them are there. What does the presence of Sljivancanin change in these circumstances, duty or no duty? It changes absolutely nothing, and there is no substantial contribution. The second part of the fifth ground deals with the fact that in his mind, did Sljivancanin know that he was going to assist the perpetrators? And the answer to this question is, absolutely, no. Could Sljivancanin reasonably believe that his commander was taking action -- not his commander, sorry, the Chief of Staff of OG South who was there was taking action? Could Sljivancanin reasonably believe that the commander of the 80 Motorised Brigade was taking action? Could he believe that all the members of the JNA who were there were taking actions? When you look at the totality of the evidence, of course he could reasonably believe that before he left Ovcara, if he was ever there. Did any of these people, were their duties modified by the fact that Sljivancanin would be in Ovcara? It had no impact whatsoever on the duty of the commander of the 80 Motorised Brigade, no impact whatsoever on Panic, no effect whatsoever on the members of JNA who are there acting, doing what they could -- what they can in the circumstances to stop the beatings, albeit insufficiently. We know that today. But at the time, they are taking action. Sljivancanin shows up there. We don't know for how long. We don't know what he sees, but we know that he could have seen that the situation was being handled. Officers senior to him are handling the situation. How can Sljivancanin ever believe that by leaving, he is going to assist the perpetrators? He can't and did not have the mens rea for aiding and abetting, even if you maintain aiding and abetting. Conclusion, Mr. President. There are two things in this case that need to be said. The first one is: When we look at the trial judgement, from a first look, it appears to be well constructed and there are many findings, but when we look at each of those findings, the way they were made, and the interaction between the findings, there are just too many contradictions, too many ifs, and too many questions left unanswered, and too many findings made by inference, that at the end of the day we don't know exactly what happened, and for this reason Sljivancanin should be acquitted. Just to use one example, the Trial Chamber uses the fact that he would have been present at Ovcara to say that he's involved in the order, and then it uses the fact that he was involved in the order to show that he was in Ovcara. We have to make a choice. Which one is the first one, and on which of these two facts do we build the responsibility of the accused? We can't in this case. Mr. President, the second thing I'd like to say has to do with the omission liability which was used by the Prosecution. The Prosecution started this case. It was joint criminal enterprise. It was ordering. It was instigating. It was insisting. It was aiding and abetting. It was everything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You really have two minutes at the utmost, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll be done in two minutes, Mr. President. It was everything but omission liability, and the case was conducted not on the basis of omission liability; it was conducted on the basis of the Prosecution's theory. At the end, the Trial Chamber unfortunately accepted this form of liability. We ask you to say that type of liability does not exist. Even if you say it does exist, there was substantial prejudice. We describe this prejudice in our pleadings, but I'll add one more. It is important to ask ourselves, why is it that we have so questions left open concerning what happened at Ovcara and what were the doings of Sljivancanin? Because the case was not conducted on the basis of omission liability, and on this basis we ask you to order a new trial, at the minimum. Either we acquit Sljivancanin and he goes home, or we have a new trial so he has the opportunity to make his case knowing what the Prosecution's case is all about. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution, you have one hour and a half. And as I indicated this morning, you don't have to use the entire time if you don't need to.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Kristina Carey. I'll be presenting the Prosecution's submissions in response to Ground 2, relating to whether aiding and abetting by omission is a mode of liability, and Ground 5, relating to the Trial Chamber's application of the elements of aiding and abetting to the facts of this case. During my submissions, I will also respond to question 4 regarding the degree of contribution required for aiding and abetting. I'll be followed by my co-counsel, Mr. Marwan Dalal, who will present the Prosecution's submissions in response to Ground 3, relating to Sljivancanin's delegated authority. Then Ms. Najwa Nabti will present the Prosecution's submissions in response to Grounds 1 and 4, relating to Sljivancanin's presence at Ovcara and what he witnessed there. For your reference, written submissions for the grounds that I will be speaking about, sub-grounds 2(a) and 2(c) and 5(a) and 5(b), are found in the Prosecution's supplemental response brief. All other written submissions for Grounds 2 and 5 are contained in the Prosecution's consolidated response brief. When the Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin, a very senior officer, delegated with the responsibility for the evacuation of Vukovar Hospital by Mile Mrksic, had breached his duty of care to protect the prisoners of war that were taken from the hospital and had knowingly assisted the TOs and paramilitaries in their torture of these prisoners by doing nothing to protect them, despite the considerable resources at his disposal, the Trial Chamber correctly characterized Sljivancanin's criminal conduct as aiding and abetting. The Trial Chamber's conclusions were sound because aiding and abetting is a mode of liability under the Statute and is criminalised in international law. Having applied the correct law, the Trial Chamber then correctly identified the elements of this mode of liability and properly applied the law to the facts. The Chamber was also correct in its conclusion that the trial was fair because Sljivancanin had notice of this theory of liability and was able to prepare a defence against it. The issue of whether aiding and abetting by omission exists in the Statute is a settled question. The Appeals Chamber, in both Oric and Brdjanin, has indicated that this mode of liability exists. The fact that the Appeals Chamber did not choose to set out the elements of aiding and abetting precisely in either Oric or Brdjanin's appeal judgements is not evidence that the mode doesn't exist under the Statute. Because the factual findings in those cases precluded entering a conviction on the basis of aiding and abetting by omission --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: I apologise. The issue had not ripened in either case. Moreover, in Oric, the Appeals Chamber stated that: "At minimum, an aider and abetter's conduct would have to meet the basic requirements of aiding and abetting." Sljivancanin's argument regarding the Appeals Chamber's language in Oric defies common sense in that it presumes that the Appeals Chamber speculated in a written judgement on the possible elements of a mode of liability that it did not believe actually existed. The Blaskic appeals judgement shows that conduct like that of Sljivancanin's in this case is criminalised and is, at the least, aiding and abetting. In Blaskic, the Appeals Chamber found that Blaskic had a duty to protect the prisoners in his custody, he knew of that duty, and was aware that the crimes were taking place. The Appeals Chamber inferred Blaskic's knowledge from the fact that he was present at the Hotel Vitez at the time that the crimes were unfolding. The fact that he took no action to discharge his duty in light of this knowledge gave rise to his criminal liability. Sljivancanin's arguments about culpable omission do not assist him, and in answer to Judge Guney's question earlier regarding commission by omission, the Prosecution submits the following: All modes of liability that include omission require that the omission be a culpable one. Culpability means only that the individual has a duty to act, knows of this duty, and fails to discharge the duty voluntarily and with the mens rea appropriate for the specific mode. For aiding and abetting, the mens rea is knowledge, which must be understood as the awareness of a probability that a crime would be committed and that the omission would assist or facilitate the commission of the crime. Sljivancanin attempts to blur the lines between culpable omission, a requirement in any mode - that includes omission - and commission by omission. This issue is settled by the Ntagerura appeals judgement. In paragraph 338, the Appeals Chamber distinguished between commission by omission, which it identified as leading to a conviction as the principal perpetrator of the crime and, quote, "aiding and abetting a crime by encouragement, tacit approval, or omission, amounting to a substantial contribution to the crime." So as you can see, both modes exist, and both require proof of a culpable omission. The Appeals Chamber has already considered the issue of the legality principle and has concluded that this mode existed under customary international law. Therefore, it is not necessary for it to take up this issue now. However, it is clear that Sljivancanin's conduct in this case, as found by the Trial Chamber, resulted in criminal liability under international law at the time that the conduct was committed. The Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin had a duty to the prisoners of war, a duty to protect them from soldiers or from anyone else while they were in his care. This duty arose under the Laws and Customs of War. The Trial Chamber further found that Sljivancanin knew that he had this duty and what it involved. The Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin witnessed the TOs and paramilitaries beating the prisoners without any intervention by the JNA forces under his command after knowing of the TOs' and paramilitaries' desire revenge themselves violently upon these prisoners, a desire they had acted upon the night before at the Velepromet facility and earlier that day at the JNA barracks. The Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin did nothing. The Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin had considerable measures at his disposal to protect the prisoners or stop the criminal acts that he saw unfolding before him, yet despite knowing that he was the officer with the greatest responsibility for these prisoners, a responsibility that had been delegated directly from Commander Mile Mrksic to him, the Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin did nothing. So was this conduct criminalised under international law in 1991? Of course it was. World War II cases make clear that culpable omissions give rise to criminality. The World War II cases do not specifically identify the mode of liability on which these convictions are based, unlike the ICTY Statute, which does distinguish between modes of liability. So in order to determine whether the mode was criminalised, it's necessary to look to the facts and holding of the case in question and then determine whether the conduct described would fall within a mode of liability in the ICTY Statute. Key World War II cases demonstrate that Sljivancanin's conduct gave rise to criminal liability. In the Essen lynching case, the accused, members of the German military, had custody of Allied airmen. They marched these airmen, prisoners of war, through an area that was populated by civilians who these members of the military knew were in a state of rage against the prisoners. The accused knew these civilians would likely take revenge against the captured prisoners should they be given the opportunity to do so. Despite being under a duty, the accused stood by and did nothing when the crowd attacked the prisoners. The Essen lynching case, the facts of which are strikingly similar to those of this case, makes clear that this conduct was criminal at the time and is criminal now. This criminalised conduct can at least be characterized as aiding and abetting under the ICTY Statute. Similarly, in the Synagogue Fire case, a member of the SS was found to have aided and abetted a crime against humanity. The Court found that the accused was liable for failing to intervene while an individual in his custody was beaten and seriously injured. The Court found that the accused was liable because having the individual in his custody gave rise to a duty to protect the person from being attacked and to prevent such attacks. This was a duty that he willfully breached by taking no action to protect the individual or deter the attacks. Again, this conduct could be characterized in our Statute at least as aiding and abetting. Sljivancanin's attempts to escape the obvious implications of these cases by arguing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Sorry, was this a duty under the 3rd Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: In the cases -- in those individual cases, no, they were not. However, the duty -- there is an ongoing duty to protect -- to treat prisoners humanely, and if Your Honours would like, I can take you through submissions with respect to the state of customary international law on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So why wasn't this directly governed by the 3rd Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: I believe in one case, the instrument that was found in the case was not the 3rd Geneva Convention, but in each case the -- I could be wrong about that, Your Honour, but my understanding, the cases each related to a duty to protect prisoners from harm, and the duty can stem or has existed - you are correct - in Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, but it has -- the duty to treat prisoners humanely has been recognised in the Lieber Code, the Brussels Declaration, the Oxford Manual, and codified in The Hague Regulations. So whether or not the individual instrument in that case was the same, the duty as clearly existed in customary international law. And if that answers Your Honour's question, I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So we are not speaking directly to the case at point now but to the history?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: If I may confer with my colleague for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Are you now talking about Sljivancanin or historical cases?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: No. In the present case, the 3rd Geneva Convention certainly applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, this is what I wanted to hear from you one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misunderstood your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So, in fact, the duties were governed by the 3rd Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And how would those duties come to an end, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, if you would be so kind, my colleague Marwan Dalal will be answering that substantially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That would be fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Sljvancanin's argument about the different sources of the duty is equally flawed. In each of these cases, the duty towards prisoners of war is the same. I, therefore, move now to the Prosecution's submissions on the Trial Chamber's articulation of the elements of this mode of liability.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber committed no error when it set out the elements of aiding and abetting by omission. The Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin had a duty to protect the prisoners of war that was imposed upon him by the Laws and Customs of War, both as part of his remit as security organ of Operations Group South and as a result of the specific authority vested upon him through Mrksic's delegation. This was a duty to act that stemmed from the rule of criminal law, in the sense that the breach of the duty results in criminal responsibility. As Blaskic makes clear, the breach of a duty to protect prisoners of war imposed by the Laws and Customs of War is criminalised both under international and domestic law, and I take Your Honours to the Blaskic appeals judgement, footnote 1384. The Trial Chamber also found that Sljivancanin had the ability to act. It found that he was in a position to take measures to stop the mistreatment of prisoners. It found that the JNA generally had sufficient resources and organisation to control the TOs and paramilitaries at all times relevant to the indictment, and it found that Sljivancanin was authorised to use, quote, "as many military police as necessary to escort the prisoners and ensure their safe passage," and that's trial judgement paragraph 396. I note as well that the Trial Chamber found that in the -- that the Guards Motorised Brigade had two battalions of military police that would have been at Sljivancanin's disposal. The Trial Chamber, therefore, correctly found that Sljivancanin's failures to act had a substantial effect on the crimes. The Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin's failure to take any steps to protect the prisoners to whom he owed a duty of care, despite his position as the senior-most officer delegated with the responsibility and authority of Commander Mrksic himself, and despite the fact that he witnessed crimes unfolding before him, had a substantial effect on the commission of the crime. Sljivancanin has failed to show how this conclusion is one that no Chamber could have reached -- I'm sorry, no reasonable Chamber could have reached. And I come now to Your Honour's fourth question. The term "concrete influence" is synonymous with the requirement that the Prosecution prove the omission had a substantial effect on the commission of the crimes. Contrary to Sljivancanin's submissions, the Prosecution is not required to prove the existence of a cause-and-effect relationship, and I apologise. Actually, that is -- he did clarify that point. It must show that the omission had a substantial effect on the crime in the sense that the crimes would have been substantially less likely had the accused acted. This was proved in this case. And, finally, the Trial Chamber applied the correct mens rea. As one can see in the Dinda-ba-hizi appeals judgement, paragraph 122, the mens rea for aiding and abetting is knowledge, which must be understood as awareness that a crime will probably be committed and that the omission will assist or facilitate the crime. In this case, however, the facts found by the Trial Chamber easily meet the standard that Sljivancanin argues for. It found that Sljivancanin knew that he had the ability to act, he knew he had the resources at his command to allow him to act effectively, and he was aware of the essential elements of the crimes that were ultimately committed by the TOs and paramilitaries. Therefore, the Trial Chamber drew the only reasonable inference to be drawn from his failure to act, given his awareness of his own ability to act, which was that Sljivancanin chose not to act. I'll turn now to Sljivancanin's arguments with respect to Ground 5. My co-counsel, Ms. Nabti, will be addressing challenges to some of the factual findings that do relate to this ground. For all other responses to challenges by the Trial Chamber's factual findings, we rely upon our response brief. My submissions, therefore, are based on the Trial Chamber's findings. The Trial Chamber's findings on each of these elements were correct and represented the only reasonable conclusions available on the evidence. The Trial Chamber correctly found that Sljivancanin's failure to take any actions to protect the prisoners of war under his care and protection had a substantial effect on the commission of tortures at the Ovcara hangar. Sljivancanin's argument incorrectly presumes that the act or omission of the aider and abetter must necessarily be known to the principal perpetrator and, thus, encourage them. This erroneous conclusion is highlighted by the fact that encouraging presence is only a subset of the forms that aiding and abetting can take. In fact, contrary to his submissions, the inactions and passivity of other individuals stands to make the impact of a forceful and effective action all the more likely to obstruct criminal conduct. He's failed to demonstrate how the inactions of other JNA personnel at Ovcara renders the Trial Chamber's conclusions about his own failure to act unreasonable. His argument that the presence of other JNA would have rendered any action that he could have taken futile disregards the Trial Chamber's findings, which were reasonable. The Chamber, in paragraph 670, found that there were steps available to Sljivancanin that would have obstructed the perpetrators' ability to commit the crimes. It found that Sljivancanin could have given clear direction to the military police at Ovcara. He could have called for more military police to come and assist at Ovcara, and he could have prevented the military police who were at Ovcara from departing when the buses departed or have called them back. These findings make clear that the fate of the prisoners did not rest solely on the competence of members of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Sljivancanin's assertions that calling upon other resources would have, quote, "taken too much time," simply has no foundation in the evidence. The Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin, through the authority delegated to him by Mrksic, had all of the resources of Operations Group South, including multiple MP battalions, at his disposal to protect these prisoners. The Trial Chamber also found in paragraph 89 that the JNA had adequate manpower, resources, and organisation to control the TOs and paramilitary threat at all relevant times. Clearly, it was objectively possible to control the criminal element at Ovcara. Sljivancanin chose not to. He argues instead that because other JNA present abdicated their responsibility or failed in their attempts to remedy the problem, he was absolved of any requirement to act. The implication of this argument is that the wholesale abdication of a duty imposed by the Laws and Customs of War is justified by the criminality, negligence, or incompetence of others. It must be rejected. The Trial Chamber's conclusion that Sljivancanin's omission facilitated the commission of the crimes was also reasonable and based on the evidence. First, the Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin witnessed the mistreatment. This finding is going to be dealt with in greater detail by my co-counsel Ms. Nabti in response to the fourth ground of appeal. In light of this finding, all of Sljivancanin's remaining arguments rely upon evidentiary speculation, which this Chamber need not engage in. However, even Sljivancanin's further speculations are at odds with the facts found by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber found that during the time that Sljivancanin was present, the JNA was taking no steps to protect the prisoners or restrain the TOs and paramilitaries. The Trial Chamber found that the presence of the TO and paramilitaries placed the prisoners at grave risk, a risk that Sljivancanin appreciated given his knowledge that these same TOs and paramilitaries had beaten prisoners bloody at the JNA barracks, requiring that the prisoners be removed from the barracks to Ovcara in order to protect them from further harm. The Chamber found that the other JNA present, such as Vojnovic, reported what they saw to Mrksic himself. However, Sljivancanin, the officer that Mrksic had entrusted with the care of these POWs, did nothing. There's no need to speculate as to whether Sljivancanin would have known and appreciated the potential value of his actions. Sljivancanin testified as to what should have been done in such a situation. And I take you now to his testimony at transcript reference 13749 through 13750, and I quote: "If he should learn that in the zone of OG South, which is a large zone, any crimes are being committed, he should order first the commander of the zone where such criminal offences are being perpetrated, be it the brigade, what measures are to be taken in order to prevent such crimes." Sljivancanin then stated: "We have agreed that it is this duty to intervene and request from the specific person responsible for the zone where the crime is being committed to take measures; if he cannot, to help him. If he cannot help him, to seek further assistance from the superior command. I think that I have been clear." Yet the Trial Chamber found that when Sljivancanin was at Ovcara and throughout the remainder of the day, despite having specific responsibility for the prisoners' safety, a duty which required that he protect them from all possible harms, whether from soldiers or other elements, and despite having all of Mrksic's own powers and authorities at his disposal to deal with the criminal threat that was so clearly posed by the TOs and paramilitaries, Sljivancanin did nothing. In light of these findings, the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Sljivancanin must have been aware that his omissions facilitated the commission of the crimes was reasonable. With respect to the issues raised by my learned colleague with respect to the indictment, the Prosecution will rest on its submissions which are contained in its brief, and this, therefore, concludes my submissions on the second and fifth grounds of appeal, and unless Your Honours have questions, I will turn the podium over to my co-counsel, Mr. Dalal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please proceed. I don't see any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Marwan Dalal, and I will be presenting the Prosecution's submissions in response to Sljivancanin's Ground 3. But before going into my submission, two brief comments, one in response to my learned colleague's proposition that only the representative of a state bears the legal duty to protect prisoners of war. Of course, we oppose this submission: Prisoners of war and the Geneva Conventions in general are too important to interpret such an important duty narrowly. We think that the legal duty to protect prisoners of war exists wherever prisoners of war are, and on -- definitely not only the representative of the state or the head of the group that have custody of the prisoners of war bears the duty to protect prisoners of war, in this case, Mile Mrksic. The legal duty and its breach is determined by the interaction with the prisoners of war and the level of awareness of violations that are being committed to prisoners of war and conduct and omission in relation to this awareness. As to the second question, when would a legal duty end, this is relevant in our context to the appeal -- to the Prosecution appeal, to the awareness of Sljivancanin and his responsibility for the murders later on the 20th-21st November, and my co-counsel Ms. Brady will deal at length on Friday when the Prosecution will submit its submission and rest its appeal on this question. I turn now to the issue of Sljivancanin's entrusted responsibility that Mrksic conferred on him on the 19th of November in the afternoon. In this regard, Sljivancanin argues that he had unlimited assignments ordered or tasked by Mrksic to him, limited to the vicinity of the hospital. Sljivancanin is wrong, in our submission, and we have answered extensively in our written brief this proposition. I will highlight several issues relating to this -- to this matter. Sljivancanin was entrusted by Mrksic on the afternoon of 19 November 1991 with the responsibility to evacuate the Vukovar Hospital the following day and transport the prisoners of war from there and be in charge of their safe passage. For this purpose, Mrksic empowered him, Sljivancanin, to use as many military police as necessary. Mrksic announced Sljivancanin's responsibility the same day during the 6.00 p.m. daily briefing at OG South Command in Negoslavci. In this, Sljivancanin's responsibility --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DALAL
utterances.text: I will slow down. Indeed, Sljivancanin's responsibility was not limited to the hospital. He was also in charge of providing safe passage to the prisoners of war. Sljivancanin acknowledged in his testimony Mrksic's order and that his responsibility in relation to the prisoners of war went beyond the hospital. The Appeals Chamber is respectfully referred to paragraphs 191, 192, 390, 396, and 400. Sljivancanin followed the path of the prisoners of war. He was at the hospital during their selection. He was at the JNA barracks when they stopped there with the buses, and he eventually was at Ovcara shortly after they arrived with the buses, the prisoners of war. The only reason for him, in our submission, to follow the prisoners of war is his responsibility to transport them safely. Both Mrksic and Sljivancanin are responsible for the crimes committed against the prisoners of war in Ovcara and before that with regard to Mrksic. Mrksic was the overall commander and was engaged with critical decisions relating to the prisoners of war. He was aware of their increasingly terrible situation in the hands of his subordinates. Sljivancanin was in charge for the entire evacuation operation as just mentioned. This entrusted responsibility by Mrksic empowered Sljivancanin to use military police as required both at the hospital and in order to transport the prisoners of war safely from there. Selection, transportation, and safety of prisoners of war were indeed inherent to the responsibility conferred on Sljivancanin by Mrksic. In this submission, I want to highlight key findings and pieces of evidence that demonstrate Sljivancanin's entrusted responsibility. Four elements will illustrate the soundness of the Chamber's finding in this regard. The first element is Sljivancanin's status and experience with a similar evacuation operation only two days before the evacuation operation in question; the second element is Sljivancanin's preparations for this operation; the third element is Sljivancanin's conduct and interaction with others at the hospital on the morning of 20 November 1991; and the last element, the fourth element, is Sljivancanin's presence at the JNA barracks that morning and at Ovcara as well as his interaction with his subordinates. The first element: Sljivancanin's status and similar operation on the 18th of November. Your Honours, at the relevant time, Sljivancanin was the senior officer, a major in the JNA. He was the chief of security organs within the OG South, which was commanded by Mrksic. Part of his responsibility as a security organ was detecting and preventing hostile activities against the armed forces. The responsibility for prisoners of war was not strange to Sljivancanin; paragraphs 115 and 668. Sljivancanin was responsible for a similar operation relating to the Croatian forces who had surrendered on 18 November 1991 at Mitnica. The destination of this group was Sremska Mitrovica, and they passed through Ovcara. Sljivancanin was the officer in command during the transport of these prisoners of war from Mitnica to Ovcara; paragraph 151. Sljivancanin's senior subordinate, Karanfilov, took a leading role in this operation. He gave instructions to and was reported to by the military police, the 80 MTBR, who secured the prisoners at Ovcara; paragraph 153, 155, and 668. Moving to the second element, Sljivancanin's preparations toward the evacuation operation. On the evening of 19 November, around 7.00 p.m., after having been entrusted by Mrksic with the responsibility for the entire evacuation operation, Sljivancanin held a briefing for his subordinates. Sljivancanin's deputy, Vukasinovic, and other senior subordinates of Sljivancanin, namely Karanfilov, and Karan attended this briefing. At this briefing, Sljivancanin ordered Vukasinovic with the organisation of transport of persons from the hospital by buses. He was to ensure the transport by buses. Shortly after 6.00 a.m. on 20 November, Vukasinovic departed from Negoslavci for Vukovar Hospital, following his superior's orders the previous day; paragraph 192 and paragraph 198. Further, at around 2.00 a.m. on 20 November, Sljivancanin met with a senior JNA colonel -- officer, Colonel Vujic, outside the command post in Negoslavci. Colonel Vujic had arrived from Belgrade to assist in handling the prisoners of war. Vujic testified, and the Trial Chamber accepted his testimony, that Sljivancanin announced at this meeting that he, Sljivancanin, would be in charge of the evacuation of the hospital the following day, paragraph 395, the evacuation of the hospital and not limited assignments at the hospital. It is clear that from the outset, Sljivancanin -- Sljivancanin's responsibility, as understood by him, was not limited to the vicinity of the hospital but extended well beyond it and included the safe transportation of prisoners of war to their final destination. The third element, Sljivancanin's conduct and interaction with others at the hospital on the morning of 20 November. Sljivancanin's conduct at the hospital clearly shows that he was in charge of the entire evacuation of the hospital. He arrived at the hospital at around 7.00 a.m., gathered the hospital staff, and told them that he would be the man in charge and the one who would be issuing orders. Colonel Vujic was also at the hospital. His accepted evidence is that Sljivancanin was giving orders to the military police present there. The accepted evidence of many witnesses at the hospital who saw Sljivancanin and interacted with him attest to his status and role; paragraph 401. Sljivancanin was the one to say who could leave the hospital compound and who could get off the buses. He was the one giving orders, and others were obeying him. The soldiers coming to him were addressing him Major, sir, or Major Sljivancanin. Everything basically transpired under his control and on his orders. The fourth element: Sljivancanin's presence at the JNA barracks and at Ovcara as well as his interaction with his subordinates. Sljivancanin's conduct and responsibility extended well beyond the hospital. From the hospital, he went to the JNA barracks when the buses with the prisoners of war were there. He was present at the JNA barracks at around 11.00, 11.30 in the morning. His presence there was not a coincidence. He went there as part of his responsibility to safely transport the prisoners of war; paragraph 372. Sljivancanin continued to exercise control over the prisoners at the JNA barracks. Prisoners listed by him were removed from the buses and returned to the hospital. There, he questioned them. Those who were thought to have participated in the fighting on the Croatian side were returned to the barracks; paragraphs 221 and 373. Sljivancanin received reports from senior subordinates of his about the deteriorating security situation of the prisoners of war at the JNA barracks to show that it was not only selection, his responsibility, but also security. His deputy, Vukasinovic, reported to him about the violent conduct of the TOs against the prisoners of war at the JNA barracks. Karanfilov also reported to Sljivancanin about what happened at the JNA barracks. Unfortunately, Sljivancanin said to Karanfilov that everything is okay. They did so, his subordinates, for one reason: Their commander, Sljivancanin, was the person in charge of safely transporting and securing the prisoners of war from the hospital; paragraphs 374 and 375. Sljivancanin's deputy, Vukasinovic, had a leading role in this operation. His role is another clear illustration of the scope of Sljivancanin's responsibility, which transcended the hospital vicinity and included the safe transportation of prisoners of war. Vukasinovic led the buses to the hospital from Negoslavci early on 20 November, following Sljivancanin's order the night before; paragraph 198. He, Vukasinovic, led the buses from the hospital to the JNA barracks at around 10.00 a.m.; paragraph 208. And eventually, Vukasinovic arrived with the buses and the prisoners of war to Ovcara at -- and this is at paragraph 259. Indeed, Your Honours, look for Vukasinovic, and you will get a clear idea about the scope of Sljivancanin's responsibility. Further, Sljivancanin was directly involved in the communication and implementation of the order to transfer the prisoners from the JNA barracks to Ovcara and to secure them there. This order, in the Chamber's finding, facilitated the commission of crimes at Ovcara that day, and this finding is solid, in our submission, and relies on other findings that are not less solid, of course. This is at paragraph 659. Indeed, Your Honours, Sljivancanin's presence at Ovcara at about 2.30, 3.00 p.m., on November 20th, not long after the arrival of the buses there from the JNA barracks, is only because he was responsible for the transportation and security of the prisoners of war. Sljivancanin was at the hospital, at the JNA barracks, and at Ovcara. Securing the safety of the prisoners of war was his responsibility, a responsibility that he manifestly failed to carry out that fatal day; paragraph 383. In conclusion, Your Honours, and based on the totality of the evidence, which I have highlighted some of it today, the only reasonable conclusion is the one reached by the Trial Chamber. Sljivancanin was ordered by Mrksic to be in charge of the entire hospital evacuation, which included necessarily the transport of the prisoners of war and securing their safe passage. Your Honours, if you have no questions on this submission, I'll turn to my co-counsel, Ms. Najwa Nabti, to present the Prosecution's response to Sljivancanin's Grounds 1 and 4 of his appeal.

utterances.speaker: MS. NABTI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will address Grounds 1 and 4 of Sljivancanin's appeal, which challenge the Trial Chamber's factual findings that Sljivancanin was present at Ovcara on 20 November 1991 and that he must have witnessed the mistreatment of prisoners there. These findings were reasonable in light of all the evidence, not just Witness P-9's identification of Sljivancanin at Ovcara, but also the timing of events on 20 November and Sljivancanin's responsibilities that day. I will not respond today to each of Sljivancanin's arguments witness by witness, which we addressed fully in our response brief. I will instead focus on a couple of main challenges he makes to the Trial Chamber's findings in Grounds 1 and 4. First, the alleged inconsistency between P-9's sightings of Sljivancanin and time-line of events on 20 November and, second, the reliability of P-9's identification of Sljivancanin at Ovcara based on Witness P-9's prior sightings of Sljivancanin and the accounts of other witnesses who did not see him. I will then turn briefly to Sljivancanin's remaining argument in Ground 4 regarding what he observed at Ovcara. On each of these main points, Sljivancanin fails to meet the standard of review on appeal. As his submissions today demonstrate, he is seeking to substitute his own assessment of the evidence for that of the Trial Chamber, disagreeing with its credibility assessments and rearguing evidence anew. This falls far short of the burden required to establish that no reasonable Chamber could have found the challenged facts, and his arguments should be rejected. Now, before getting into the specific's of P-9's sighting of Sljivancanin at Ovcara on 20 November 1991, it's useful to provide some context for the events of that day, particularly since Sljivancanin argues that he could not have been seen at Ovcara or the JNA barracks by P-9 because he was somewhere else at the time. The Trial Chamber's findings make it clear that P-9's sightings of Sljivancanin on 20 November are, in fact, consistent with the estimated time-line of events that day, taking into account Sljivancanin's presence at other locations and the distances between those locations. The Defence referred to Exhibit 156, which is a map, and that confirms that the distance between Vukovar Hospital and the JNA barracks is less than four kilometres. The distance between the hospital and Ovcara is less than ten kilometres. The Trial Chamber found that these locations were not far apart at paragraphs 222 and 223, and while it may have taken a convoy of five buses of prisoners a half an hour to get from the JNA barracks to Ovcara, it wouldn't necessarily take Sljivancanin that same amount of time. But even so, it would still be consistent with the Chamber's findings on the time-line of events. With that in mind, I turn first to the events of the morning of November 20, 1991. And as will be appearing before you, at 10.30 in the morning, five buses of prisoners from Vukovar, the Vukovar Hospital, arrived at the JNA barracks. Around this same time -- around the same time, Sljivancanin met international monitors at Vukovar Hospital after having blocked them at a nearby bridge while the buses of prisoners departed the hospital. About 20 minutes later at the barracks, a group of 12 to 15 prisoners identified as hospital employees or family members were transferred to an empty military bus, referred to as the sixth bus, which then returned to the hospital after some time. At around 11.00 or 11.30, Sljivancanin was seen at the barracks shortly before this sixth bus departed, and before noon, Sljivancanin was back at the hospital to screen the passengers from the sixth bus together with TO Commander Vujovic, who had also just been at the JNA barracks. Moving to the afternoon, around 1300 or 1400, Sljivancanin was interviewed in front of Vukovar Hospital by a news team. Around 1330 or 1430, five buses of prisoners arrived at Ovcara, and they were unloaded one by one, each taking about 15 to 20 minutes.
