Around 1400 or 1430, Sljivancanin was at the hospital when the last buses of civilians departed. And at around 1430 or 1500, Sljivancanin was seen standing down the road from the hangar at Ovcara. This time-line is not only consistent with the relatively short distances involved; as the Chamber found at paragraph 372 and also as my co-counsel, Mr. Dalal, has highlighted, it makes sense that Sljivancanin would check on the status of the evacuation of these prisoners, given his responsibilities that day. Indeed, Sljivancanin knew that TOs and paramilitaries had attacked this group of prisoners that was transferred at the barracks in the morning, and this was despite the presence of JNA officers and military police; trial judgement paragraph 375. Even by Sljivancanin's own account, Vukasinovic warned Sljivancanin that he, quote, "had problems in the barracks because members of the Territorial Defence think that you are releasing the most notorious Ustashas and that you did that last night at Mitnica too." Sljivancanin transcript pages 13656 to 13657. So Sljivancanin was aware that unlike the previous evacuation of Croat prisoners from Mitnica to Sremska Mitrovica, this time the TOs knew about and were violently opposing the evacuation of prisoners. He, therefore, had reason to check on the status of the evacuation that afternoon, particularly once the buses of civilians left the hospital. To sum up, the Trial Chamber's estimated time-line of events on 20 November 1991 is consistent with P-9's sightings of Sljivancanin that day. I'll now address the Defence's challenge to P-9's identification of Sljivancanin at Ovcara based on P-9's prior sightings of Sljivancanin and the accounts of other witnesses. Despite what the Defence has argued, the Trial Chamber did address the reliability of P-9's identification and noted, in particular, that P-9 had seen Sljivancanin up close on two previous occasions; the day before at Vukovar Hospital and that very morning at the JNA barracks. Sljivancanin was indeed a memorable figure. P-9 recalled his distinctively different appearance and his commanding presence, which left a strong impression on P-9. So when P-9 saw Sljivancanin for a third time at Ovcara, there is no question that this was the same JNA officer; trial judgement paragraphs 367 to 368, 377, and 383. Indeed, as another witness confirmed, Sljivancanin, quote, "was so striking that I don't think it's possible to forget a man like that." Berghofer, transcript page 5278. As addressed fully in our response brief, the Chamber's findings on P-9's previous sightings of Sljivancanin were also reasonable. Although I'll touch further on Sljivancanin's presence at the JNA barracks when addressing Sljivancanin's argument about the observations of other witnesses, for now I'd like to point out that the Trial Chamber carefully analysed and explained why it found other witnesses' testimonies did not contradict P-9's sighting of Sljivancanin at the JNA barracks on 20 November, and this is in paragraphs 369 to 372. P-9's sighting of Sljivancanin at Vukovar Hospital on 19 November was likewise reasonable and consistent with other witnesses' evidence that Sljivancanin was there that afternoon; Trial Chamber judgement paragraphs 183 and 367. I'll turn now to the Defence's challenge to the Trial Chamber's reliance on P-9's evidence based on the testimonies of other witnesses. The thrust of his argument is that because other witnesses didn't see Sljivancanin at the JNA barracks and Ovcara and P-9 did, the Chamber's reliance on P-9's testimony must be unreasonable. This argument also lacks merit. The Trial Chamber looked at all the evidence about P-9's sightings of Sljivancanin on 20 November. It made detailed findings about what other witnesses saw and didn't see, considering the different times and locations from where these witnesses' observations were made. For example, at the JNA barracks, at paragraphs 296 to 298 and 370, the Trial Chamber canvassed the different times and locations that various JNA officers were at the barracks on the morning of the 20th and explained why they may not have seen Sljivancanin in light of their differing accounts. The Chamber further considered, at paragraphs 216 and 369, that the prisoners at the barracks were being threatened by TOs and paramilitaries surrounding the buses and were not in a position to recognise all persons near the buses at some time. Further detail is provided in our briefs. Regarding the witnesses at Ovcara, the Trial Chamber provided more than ten pages of analysis, addressing the various accounts of the JNA officers, including P-14, Vojnovic, and Panic. The specific arguments are addressed in our response brief, but for each of them the Chamber addressed when they were at Ovcara, for how long, where they were, whether they went inside the hangar, what they were doing, and who they saw. The Chamber then reasonably explained why these testimonies did not call in question the evidence of P-9, based on their differing locations, timing, and perspectives. In particular, several of them were only at Ovcara for only a short time, and others went inside the hangar; trial judgement paragraphs 254 to 274 and 378 to 383. The Trial Chamber further considered that the prisoners at Ovcara were not in the position to notice the presence of all JNA officers outside the hangar. The Chamber also considered the effects of fear and the chaotic situation on these witnesses; trial judgement paragraphs 234, 236 to 238, and 382. Indeed, at the time that Sljivancanin was found to be at Ovcara, they were either being beaten in the gauntlet or already inside the hangar. The testimonies of these witnesses as cited in our response brief confirm this, and they leave no doubt that their primary focus was on survival and avoiding the beatings at this time. I would like to respond to one point made by the Defence today, which requires us to move briefly into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NABTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Sljivancanin has dwelt at some length on the alleged inconsistency between the evidence P-9 and Hajdar Dodaj, a JNA deserter who was pulled off one of the buses at Ovcara, but as their testimonies make clear, the different perspectives of these two witnesses show that their testimonies are not contradictory and that the Trial Chamber was entitled to rely on both. P-9 testified that he saw Sljivancanin standing on the road leading to the hangar, whereas Dodaj testified that he and other JNA deserters stood to the right of the hangar -- hangar's entrance, with the hangar's door and the gauntlet in between. Each witness marked a photograph of Ovcara to show their locations on 20 November, and I'd like to pull those up for you now, Your Honour. Just as a side note, the red markings on this exhibit were made by the witnesses, and the white markings were added for emphasis by us. The first exhibit is 282, marked by Witness P-9. He used the letter "B" to show where the buses unloaded, and the two lines mark the gauntlet leading to the hangar's entrance. After arriving at Ovcara, P-9 went to the back of the hangar for about 15 to 20 minutes and stood in the spot marked "C." As he returned to the front of the hangar, he saw Sljivancanin standing on the road in the place marked with a "D." Those explanations are given by P-9 at transcript pages 6176 to 6177. The next exhibit, number 238, was marked by Witness Dodaj to reflect where he was standing in relation to the hangar's entrance. Number "1" marks the place where he and other JNA deserters were standing until they left Ovcara. The "2" marks where he and the last bus -- where he saw the last bus unloading in front of the hangar. Those explanations are given in Dodaj's testimony at pages 5661 to 5663. Now, clearly, these two witnesses had different vantage points. Remember that even following the gauntlet armed with TOs and paramilitaries continued to go in and out of the hangar's entrance, between where Dodaj was standing and the place where P-9 saw Sljivancanin. The Trial Chamber considered these different vantage points and also expressly considered Dodaj's testimony that he did not see Sljivancanin at Ovcara in evaluating the evidence of another JNA deserter who was standing right next to Dodaj at the time. Those findings are at trial judgement paragraphs 384 to 385. These exhibits and testimony leave no question that these witnesses had different vantage points. Indeed, the Trial Chamber's detailed findings show that it carefully evaluated the testimony of all these witnesses, who are also engulfed in a chaotic situation. It was not unreasonable to find that these testimonies did not undermine P-9's sighting of Sljivancanin at Ovcara. Indeed, the Trial Chamber considered the very factors this Chamber found relevant in assessing witness testimony in the Nata-Kiru-Timana appeal judgement of 13 December 2004. At page 286, the Appeals Chamber found: "The fact that several witnesses were in the same general area does not necessarily mean their observations about the identity and location of those present have to be identical for the witnesses to be considered credible. The difference in their respective statements can be explained by the place from where these witnesses made their observations as well as the fact that witnesses did not give exact times for their observations." In addition to these factors, the Trial Chamber reasonably explained why it could not fully accept the testimony of some witnesses, including Sljivancanin's direct subordinates, Vukasinovic and Karanfilov, and those findings with respect to Vukasinovic are at paragraphs 192 and 259 to 260, and 379, and for Karanfilov, at paragraphs 216, 278, 282, and 300. All of the testimony the Defence relies on today and in its briefs was before the Trial Chamber and was duly considered. In short, the Defence has not shown that the Trial Chamber's reliance on P-9's identification of Sljivancanin at Ovcara is one that no reasonable Chamber could have made. I'll turn finally to respond to Sljivancanin's main challenge in Ground 4. The Defence argues that there was no omission because the Trial Chamber erred in finding that Sljivancanin must have witnessed the mistreatment of prisoners in the gauntlet at Ovcara. This is phrased as a challenge to the finding of an omission, but it's clear that Sljivancanin is really challenging the Chamber's mens rea findings. As my co-counsel Ms. Carey has mentioned earlier, the Trial Chamber found that Sljivancanin had the necessary mens rea. He knew the beatings and tortures would occur based on a number of factors considered together, at paragraphs 663 to 666, including that Sljivancanin knew of prior reports that local TOs and paramilitaries in Vukovar killed and mistreated Croatian prisoners and committed sadistic abuse and acts of revenge. He knew of the attack on the prisoners at the JNA barracks earlier in the day, and he witnessed the TOs and paramilitaries beating the prisoners in the gauntlet at Ovcara and further observed their free access to the prisoners in the hangar. These findings make clear that Sljivancanin's witnessing of the gauntlet was only one of the factors proving Sljivancanin's knowledge of the torture and mistreatment at Ovcara, and this makes sense. It can't be right, as Sljivancanin argues, that an accused who had this level of knowledge would not realise that he had a duty to act unless and until he actually saw the prisoners being beaten before his very eyes. So what did Sljivancanin observe at Ovcara? First, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that the gauntlet was still happening at the time Sljivancanin arrived at Ovcara, so he would have witnessed the unrestrained beating of the prisoners. It found that P-9 arrived at Ovcara when the last two buses of prisoners were unloading. While this unloading was still in progress, P-9 went to the back of the hangar. That's at trial judgement 377 and P-9 transcript page 6163. When P-9 returned from the back of the hangar about 15 minutes later, he saw Sljivancanin looking on the road towards the hangar, looking very angry -- I'm sorry, standing on the road, looking very angry. There were no more prisoners entering the hangar at that time; trial judgement paragraphs 377 and 383. It was reasonable for the Chamber to conclude that Sljivancanin witnessed the beatings in the gauntlet. It's highly unlikely that Sljivancanin instantaneously appeared only for the moment that P-9 saw him. Prisoners were still unloading when P-9 went to the back of the hangar, and each bus took 15 to 20 minutes to unload, and Sljivancanin had every reason to be there. He was the person in command of the evacuation of these prisoners and vested with the responsibility for their security. Another important detail is that Sljivancanin looked very angry, the obvious inference being that he was reacting to seeing something other than a peaceful and secure situation in front of the hangar. Indeed, Sljivancanin had a similar reaction earlier that day when a group of TOs confronted him at the hospital. In Sljivancanin's own words, they, quote, "expressed their revolt" to the removal of a few prisoners from the buses at the barracks. Sljivancanin had to instruct TO Commander Vujovic to, quote, "warn his people not to behave toward me in an unsoldierly way." Sljivancanin transcript pages 13656 to 13657. At Ovcara, the TOs and paramilitaries were again out of control. On all the evidence, the Chamber's finding that Sljivancanin witnessed the gauntlet beatings was reasonable. In any event, even if Sljivancanin did not personally witness this as he alleges and as he alleges that he arrived after the prisoners were already in the hangar, the Trial Chamber's findings about what was occurring at Ovcara leave no doubt that he still must have known the prisoners were being mistreated. Your Honours, picture the scene that he was confronted with. The Chamber found at paragraph 235 that there was no intervention by the military police on the buses before they left, nor by the 15 to 20 JNA soldiers in front of the hangar, to try to stop the beatings. At this time, as the Chamber found, the freedom of the TOs and paramilitaries to freely enter the hangar was too obvious. In other words, anyone present at Ovcara would have seen this and would have also seen that many of these men were armed and had heightened emotions; Trial Chamber paragraphs 309 and 663. The beatings of the prisoners did not stop with the gauntlet, either. They continued relentlessly for some time after the prisoners entered the hangar. They were so severe that the cries of prisoners being beaten could be heard from outside the hangar; trial judgement paragraphs 237 to 235. Also at this time, the Chamber found at paragraph 238 that TOs and paramilitaries were moving in and out of the hangar as they took turns beating the prisoners in intervals, and the security outside the hangar was also plainly obvious -- plainly insufficient. Even from the outside, anyone could see that there was a disproportionately large number of TOs and paramilitaries compared with the relatively small number of JNA soldiers; trial judgement paragraphs 245, 309, and 625. The point is, this evident lack of security and beatings by TOs and paramilitaries continued well after the unloading of the prisoners through the gauntlet, which would undoubtedly cover the time that P-9 saw Sljivancanin on the road in front of the hangar, and even if this was only for a moment, it would have been enough for Sljivancanin to take in this scene and understand its meaning. In these circumstances, there's no question that Sljivancanin knew that the prisoners were being mistreated and tortured and that these crimes would continue unless he intervened, whether or not he witnessed the gauntlet. In conclusion, the Chamber's findings that Sljivancanin was present at Ovcara on 20 November and must have witnessed the mistreatment of prisoners there are reasonable on all the evidence. Based on everything that Sljivancanin saw and knew at that time, he was clearly aware that prisoners would be mistreated and tortured at Ovcara unless he took action. His arguments in 1 and 4 should be -- in Grounds 1 and 4 should be dismissed. Unless there are any questions, Your Honours, those are my submissions.
